div.head: SCENE I.

sp.speaker: Tom.
sp.p: Ha, ha, ha! What a guy you look! Where the deuce did you pick up that livery?

sp.speaker: Bit.
sp.p: Excuse me, Master Thomas, it ain't no livery at all. Mrs. Sparsit gave me the choice of three liveries a-year, or to find my own undress suit, and have five pounds additional wages instead. I preferred the latter, and dress economically, as you see. That's a fact.

sp.speaker: Tom.
sp.p: That's right. Nothing but facts—as my father says—facts, nothing but facts, root out everything else. I must proceed into the counting-house, and that directly. I say, bon jour, Maitre Bits.

sp.speaker: Bit.
sp.p: And I say, go to the devil with your bon jour, or jaw of any kind. I'm a simple man, and only understand my native language.

sp.speaker: Tom.
sp.p: There, don't be cross.
You should not sing, Bitz; you have but an indifferent voice.

sp.speaker: Bit.
sp.p: Who asked you to stay and hear it?

sp.speaker: Tom.
sp.p: Nobody. But Mr. Bounderby desired me to stay here till he came in.

sp.speaker: Bit.
sp.p: Then, pray, go into the garden and drive the birds from the fruit, that you may say you have, once in your life, been of some use.

sp.speaker: Tom.
sp.p: The garden! It's far too hot to go there.

sp.speaker: Bit.
sp.p: You may bathe in the pond, then. There's a little water in it—and plenty of mud.

sp.speaker: Tom.
sp.p: My sister Loo says she'll have that pond removed.

sp.speaker: Bit.
sp.p: What's that? What did you say?

sp.speaker: Tom.
sp.p: I said—the pond must be removed. When the banker marries Loo, you will see.

sp.speaker: Bit.
sp.p: Your master marry Miss Louisa!

sp.speaker: Tom.
sp.p: Yes. Mr. Bounderby will forget what is due to her illustrious ancestors.

sp.speaker: Bit.
sp.p: But Miss Louisa won't forget what is due to herself, I hope.

sp.speaker: Tom.
sp.p: Be more respectful, Bitz. If I say one word to my master, you will lose his favour.

sp.speaker: Bit.
sp.p: So!

sp.speaker: Tom.
sp.p: Indeed, I doubt whether the banker will keep you in his service at all.

sp.speaker: Bit.
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: Tom.
sp.p: What does he pay you for?

sp.speaker: Bit.
sp.p: Since you come to that, what does Mr. Bounderby pay you for? It is now near noon, and the books wait your coming.

sp.speaker: Tom.
sp.p: Well, that's no business of yours. If I like to stay, I'll stay, for all the rich bankers in the world.

sp.speaker: Bit.
sp.p: Well, it's no business of mine; but, as both my master and mistress are coming this way, perhaps you'll say as much in their presence.
Please, sir, the clerk says as how—

sp.speaker: Tom.
sp.p: Hush! I must be off, in earnest; but only wait till I catch you alone again, that's all.

sp.speaker: Bit.
sp.p: I suppose I must follow his example, and make myself scarce, or come in for the share of abuse intended for him.

div.stage: [Exit Bitzer, as Bounderby and Mrs. Sparsit enter.

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: My dear madam! I hadn't a shoe to my foot! As to a stocking, I didn't know such a thing, by name! Nay, I was born in a ditch!

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: I hope it was a dry one.

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: As wet as a sop. A pool of stagnant water in it.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: Dear me! Enough to give you your death of cold.

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: I was born with inflammation of the lungs. I was so sickly, that I was always moaning and groaning. I was so ragged and dirty, you wouldn't have touched me with a pair of tongs. How I fought through it, I don't know. But I did fight through it, however; and here I am, and nobody to thank but myself.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: Some thanks, I hope, sir, to your mother?

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: Mother? Bolted, madam!

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: Bolted! I see; bolted the chamber door to lock you safely in of nights, I suppose?

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: No; left me to the care of my grandmother, who was the wickedest and the worse old woman that ever lived. If I got a new pair of shoes, by any accident, she would take them off my feet, and sell them for drink. I have known that grandmother of mine lie a-bed and drink her fourteen glasses of rum and water before swallowing a bit of breakfast.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: How shocking! My heart bleeds for you.

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: She kept a chandler's shop, she did, and fed me in an egg-box. That was my cradle—an old worn-out egg-box, full of splints and nails. As soon as I was big enough to run away, of course I ran away. Then I became a young vagabond; and, instead of one old woman knocking me about, I was knocked about and starved by everybody—I was, madam.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: Your early fate in life sickens me to the heart, sir.

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: But I pulled through it, though nobody threw me a rope. Vagabond, errand-boy, vagabond, labourer, porter, clerk, chief manager, small partner, head partner, Josiah Bounderby, of Coketown upon Coketown. These are the antecedents and calumniations. I learnt my letters from the outsides of the shops, and was first able to tell the time upon the dial-plate, from studying the steeple clock of St. Giles's Church, under the direction of a drunken cripple, who was an incorrigible thief and a vagabond. You may force me to swallow burning fat, you may, but you can never force me to suppress the facts of my life.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: Ingenuous creature! What nobility of soul! To confess so much to me, too!

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: Ay; but, perhaps, I'm wrong. What do you want to know about these sort of things? At the time when, to have been a shoeblack, would have been a godsend to me—a prize in the lottery, you were coming out of the Italian Opera in satin and jewels, a blaze of splendour, when I hadn't a penny to buy a link with, to light you home.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: I certainly was familiar with the opera, at a very early age.

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: Egad! so was I—with the wrong side of it. A hard pavement at the back of the opera in the Arcade; a very hard bed I had of it. But what do you know of these matters? I ought to speak to you about May Fair, of lords and of ladies, of honourables, and of right honourables.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: It is not necessary for you to do anything of the kind, sir. I hope I have learned how to accommodate myself to the changes in life.

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: But you must confess, madam, that you were born in the lap of luxury.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: I cannot deny that.

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: Enjoyed crack society—devilish high society.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: Admitted.

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: The very tip-top of fashion, and all that sort of thing.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: Unquestionably, true.

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: A most amazing height, from which you could look down upon me, and say that the dirtiest part about me is—

sp.speaker: Bit.
sp.p: One of your hands, sir.

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: What can one of my hands want with me so early—

sp.speaker: Bit.
sp.p: Not knowing, I cannot say, sir; but, judging from appearances, I imagine—

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: Hold your tongue, sir! Well, as it is one of the hands, have the goodness to tell the hand to make use of his feet, and walk up. Now, madam, if the rude interruption is not too much for your nerves.
Oh! it's you, Stephen. What's the matter with you? We have never had any difficulty with you, and you have never been unreasonable. I know already you do not come here to make a complaint.

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.p: Noa, sir. I ha' coom for now't o' the koind.

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: You are a steady hand, and I was not mistaken. Now, let us hear what you come for, and what it is all about.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: I can go, Mr. Bounderby, if you require it. I would not intrude, for the world.

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: Now, you see, Stephen, this lady is a bred and born lady—a very high lady. You are not to suppose, because she condescends to keep my house, that she is not very high up the tree. I told you she is—ay, to the top of the tree. Now, if what you have to say cannot be said before a bred and born lady, this lady will leave the room; if, however, what you have to say can be said before a bred and born lady, this lady will stay where she is.

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.p: Sir; I hope I never had now't to say not fitten for a bred and born lady to hear, sin' I were born mysel'.

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: Then, fire away.

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.p: I be coom to ask advice, sir. I ha' been married nineteen year to a lass, a young cratur', that has gone bad like—not along of me; no. Gonnows, I am not an unkind husband to her.

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: I have heard of this before. Your wife found other companions, took to drinking, left off working, sold your furniture, pledged your clothes.

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.p: Yes; I were patient with her.

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: The more fool you! Go on—go on.

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.p: I tried to wean her from it, ower and ower again. I tried this, and I tried that—I tried t'other. Many's the time I ha' gone home, and found all vanished—all that I had in the world, all that I had been saving for years; and her, without sense left to bless herself, lying on the bare boards, insensible to sheam or rebuke. And then she went from bad to worse; from worse, to worse still. She left me. She disgraced herself; but she coom back, and what was I to do to hinder her? I ha' walked about the streets all night, rather than go home—ay, night after night! And I ha' e'en gone to bridge, minded to throw myself in, and end at once my misery.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: Shocking! Disgraceful creature!

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.p: I ha' paid her to keep away from me— these five good years I ha' paid her to do so. I ha' gotten decent, tidy furniture again, and was not sheamed or fearful o' the other minnits of my life, but she came back last night, and she says she be come—for what? She become to sell off all I ha' got in the world. Now, sir, I ask you, how I am to be rid of this woman? I mon be ridden o' her. I canna' bear it, and I won't. But for the pitying words, and kind consolation of the best lass in the world, living or dead, I must ha' gone mad long ago.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: How indecorus! I see it all, sir; he wishes to free himself to marry the woman of whom he is speaking, sir.

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.p: You be right—I do; I were a coming to that. It's more than I can bear; and yet, if I do her any hurt, there's a law to punish me.

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: Of course there is.

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.p: If I flee from her—constable can bring me back.

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: Of course he can.

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.p: And if I refuse any longer to support her, or find her money for drink, and tak' myself to another part of the country, board o' guardians can charge me with desertion, and clap me into prison.

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: Of course they can.

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.p: If I marry t'other lass, I may be punished.

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: Decidedly.

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.p: Hanged, perhaps?

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: No; the punishment is not so severe as that. But a long imprisonment would await you.

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.p: In the name of heaven, show me the law to help me!

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: No; don't ask me to show you law; consult a respectable solicitor. He'll bring you and your wife into open court; and in that way, perhaps, you'll get a remedy.

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.p: Perhaps! It be not certain, then?

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: There is no certainty in the law, man.

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.p: What be the use of going to law, then?

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: Oh! you may have luck—a hundred things, if you don't mind publicity.

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.p: Pub—what? Oh, I know. Against all the world with my misery, and be the laughing-stock of all the bawds of the whole town—of everybody.

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: Well, if you wish to be divorced—

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.p: Can it be done in private, loike?

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: Certainly not.

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.p: Then I say it's a downright burning—
It's a muddle altogether, and the sooner I am dead, the better.

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: Pooh, pooh! Don't you talk about things you don't understand; and don't call, in my presence, the glorious institutions of your country a muddle, or you'll get yourself into a muddle—a real muddle, one of these fine mornings. You took your wife for better and for worse; if she has turned out worse, why all we have got to say is, she might have turned out better.

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.p: Must I pay lawyer-chap?

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: Of course you must.

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.p: How much?

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: Can't say. The divorce court is an expensive luxury. Besides, you must be prepared with direct proof. I don't think mere inebriety—

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.p: Ay; as I said before, it's all a muddle.

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: Harkye, sirrah; you have been quite shocking this lady, whom I have told you is a real lady, a bred and born lady, with your unhallowed opinions. Now you have always been a steady hand; but my opinion is—and I tell you plainly,—you are turning from the right road, and the best thing you can do is to come out of it. I can see as far into a grindstone as any other— father than many, perhaps, because I had my nose well kept to it when I was young. I see traces of turtle soup and venison, and gold spoons, in all this. I do, by the Lord Harry, I do!

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.p: Sir, sir! since I canna' get help or consolation from you, I shall return to my work, and think how I am to be rid of her.
What be the neame of lawyer-chap you recommend I to go to?

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: I recommend! I do nothing of the sort. I beg you'll mention my name in nothing of the kind. I'm known as a rich man, and a powerful man, hereabouts; and who knows but, from sheer envy and spite, the pettifogging rascals of this town might induce you to make me a co-respondent in your particular case. Oh, my dear Mrs. Sparsit.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: Shocking! Dreadful! Abominable!

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.p: What he means, be all Greek to me; but if there be justice in the land, I'll sell all off to get it, and thanks to nobody.

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: Gone! Not even a bow to me, or a bend of the head to you, ma'am, a bred and born lady? Did you notice that, madam?

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: That man means mischief, Mr. Bounderby.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Beg pardon, sir; but didn't you come out of that gentleman's house? I think it was you, unless I have had the bad luck to mistake the person I was watching.

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.p: Yes, missus—it were I.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Excuse an old woman's curiosity, but have you seen the banker?

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.p: Oh, yes; I have seen him.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: How did he look, sir? Was he well and hearty?

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.p: Yes—all that.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: And jolly?

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: And what might the great man be doing?

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.p: He were eating and drinking. He be great indeed. He's as large and as long as a hommoa-bee.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: I am glad to hear it. Thank ye, thank ye.

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.p: From the country, I suppose, missus?

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: By parliamentary this morning. I came forty odd mile by parliamentary this morning, and I shall go back the same forty odd mile by parliamentary this afternoon. I walked nine long mile to the station; and if I find nobody to give me a lift, I shall walk nine long mile back to-night, which, I think, is pretty well at my time of life.

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.p: Indeed it is. Don't do it too often, missus.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: No, no; only once a-year. I spend my savings so once in every year. I come regularly once a-year to walk about the streets, and see all the fine gentlemen.

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.p: What! only to see them?

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Quite enough for me—I ask no more. I have been standing about on this side of the way since I arrived in the morning, in hopes of seeing Mr. Bounderby come out of the Bank. But, however, as I have seen you, and you've seen him, I must make that do as well.
What! sighing, sir; ain't you happy?

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.p: Nobody but has their troubles, missus.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: You may say that yours be at home, perhaps?

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.p: They be.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Yet working under such a great gentleman, they do not follow you to the factory.

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.p: No; they hadn't need to follow me there.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: One question more, if you please. How long have you worked in that great factory?

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.p: Twelve years or so, I should say.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Twelve years! I must kiss the head that has worked twelve long years in that fine factory!
Good-bye, good-bye! We may meet again. Twelve long years! Only think!

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.p: Bless thee, Rachel! I know thee would'st come. You are early, lass—early.

sp.speaker: Rac.
sp.p: I am a little too early at times, and a little too late at times; but, early or late, I do come, although I am never to be counted upon.

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.p: Come when you will, 'tis a happy time to me.

sp.speaker: Rac.
sp.p: Yes, lad; and to me the same. We are such true friends, and such old friends, and getting to be such old folks too.

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.p: To me, Rachel, thou art as young as ever thou wast.

sp.speaker: Rac.
sp.p: 'Tis better not to walk too much together, lad; you know my reason.

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.p: Right, Rachel, right. Go thy ways. I won't be keeping thee from thy work, but let me have the blessing of thy smile when work be done.
She has been that to me for so many years, and has done me so much good, and cheered me so like, that her word is law to me—better than some real ones. Heaven reward her kindness!

div.head: SCENE III.
div.stage: RACAEL discovered sitting by the side of a small bed, the curtains of which are drawn close. BITZER is at the door, carrying a basket, in the act of leaving.

sp.speaker: Bit.
sp.p: Any message to missus?

sp.speaker: Rac.
sp.p: My compliments to Mrs. Sparsit, and I thank her for the medicine. I will see the poor creature takes it regulary.

sp.speaker: Bit.
sp.p: Master never comes here himself, then?

sp.speaker: Rac.
sp.p: Mr. Bounderby! Oh, dear no; that would indeed be a condescension.

sp.speaker: Bit.
sp.p: It's all right. What a fidgetty creature missus is. I expect there's a little of the green-eyed monster in this sudden fit of kindness; but it's no affair of mine.
Now, then, Mr. Hands, where are you pushing a body?

sp.speaker: Rac.
sp.p: Hush! tread softly. Don't be alarmed, she has not hurt herself seriously. I have dressed her wound, and she has fallen into a dose. Mrs. Sparsit has kindly sent me some medicine, and she said somebody wanted looking to, and she was right. All wandering, and lost and bruised as she is, there are hopes yet of saving her.

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.p: Noa, noa. Heaven help me, she will drive me mad!

sp.speaker: Rac.
sp.p: I have done what little I could for her, and I am willing to do more. We worked together at the same frame when we were girls. I came cheerfully, Stephen; for I know your heart, lad, and am certain sure it is too merciful to let her suffer for want of aid.

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.p: She has made me the jest and gibe—the sport —of all the hands in the factory, and it is more than I can bear. I shall be driven to do something desperate—I know I shall.

sp.speaker: Rac.
sp.p: You must not talk so, Stephen. Come, you are tired, and must want sleep. I will stay and keep watch till the bell goes three. I slept sound last night, and want but little rest. Try to sleep, dear, dear Stephen, if it be only to get a nap on your chair. I'll watch and tend to her.

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.p: Kind, kind, Rachel!

sp.speaker: Rac.
sp.p: When she gets better, Stephen, it's to be hoped she'll mend, and do thee no more hurt or injury, we will hope.
Poor lad, he has fallen asleep at last. I hope his short sleep will not be disturbed. It shall not, if I can help it.

May it be happy and sound. I'll throw this kerchief over, for he's getting chilly and cold. Let me recollect. I am to bathe her temples every two hours; it must be near the time. I'll do as the doctor directed, and then she may be safely let till the morning.
How unlucky, the chimes have awakened Stephen.

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.p: Rachel, Rachel! such a dream! Why did'st you wake me up? Oh, such a dream! Methought 'twas marriage morn wi' Margaret, and she were good again. Church bells were ringing, birds were carolling, and everything looked gay and bright. There she was, virtuous and blooming as the day we first met, hanging on my arm, and I the envy of every hand that had turned out to wish us joy. And there, uncommon plain, amongst the lot, stood the grey-headed, feeble man, more joyous than the rest, her father—Rachel, her father! He stood blessing us; and blessing us, till the tears streamed down his aged face. The same old man I knew in life full twenty years bygone. There he was, and uttering the self-same words, “Avoid drink, Stephen; and gi' none to Margaret.” These were the words; and thee dost know, Rachel, I have throughout my life shunned it, and put it away from her; but she got it, and she broke that old man's heart, as she is breaking mine; but she sha'n't, she sha'n't! I will not be a mark of scorn for all the hands to point at. No! she has brought me to this, and she must bide the consequence!

div.stage: (Stephen seizes a gun, which is suspended over the door, and is making towards the bed, when Rachel snatches it from him, and points upwards.)

sp.speaker: Rac.
sp.p: Rash, inconsiderate man! It is now your turn to ask forgiveness. There.

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.p: Rachel, thou changest me from bad to good. Thou makest me wish to be more like thee. Rachel, I were standing on a brink, but thou hast saved me. I came home desperate wi'out a hope—I dreamt—oh, such a dream! It took me back to what I was. I woke from what I was, to look at what I am. My fevered brain could not bear it. I saw the only end of all my miseries. Rachel, I never hurt a human creature. I saw the gun. I thought of her. I thought of you!

sp.speaker: Rac.
sp.p: And never once of him?

div.head: SCENE I.
div.stage: —Chamber in the House of Mr. Gradgrind.

sp.speaker: Lou.
sp.p: Well, you're a stranger. What a time it is since you last came to see me!

sp.speaker: Tom.
sp.p: I've been busily engaged, and that's the truth, of an evening; but, in the day-time, old Bounderby has been keeping me at it rather late. But I touch him up with you now and then, when he comes it too strong, and so we preserve an understanding. I say, Loo, has father said anything particular to you?

sp.speaker: Lou.
sp.p: Only, that he had something to communicate to me in the morning.

sp.speaker: Tom.
sp.p: That's just what I mean. Do you know where he is to-night?

sp.speaker: Lou.
sp.p: I do not.

sp.speaker: Tom.
sp.p: I will tell you. He's with Mr. Bounderby, having a confab at the Bank. Why at the Bank, yon'll say? I'll tell you: it's to keep Mr. Sparsit's ears off, as far as possible. I say, Loo; you are fond of me, ain't you?

sp.speaker: Lou.
sp.p: Indeed, I am; though you seldom come to see me.

sp.speaker: Tom.
sp.p: Well, sister of mine; if you would make up your mind to do, I know what, it would be such a splendid thing for me—I should be uncommon jolly.

sp.speaker: Lou.
sp.p: I should be glad to see you in spirits any time, Tom.

sp.speaker: Tom.
sp.p: Well, Loo; I thought I'd just run down, and give you a hint of what is going on, though I suppose you would not likely guess, if you did not ever know. I cannot stay now to explain, because I give a feast to some fellows to-night, and must scrape up the tin.
I say, Loo; you can't lend me a fiver, can you? Oh, lud! here comes the governor—I must cut.

sp.speaker: Mr. G.
sp.p: Louisa, my dear; you have been so well trained, act so little on the impulsive, and are so very far from the romantic, that I know you will well weigh and consider what I am about to say and communicate. You are the subject of a proposal of marriage!

sp.speaker: Lou.
sp.p: Marriage, sir!

sp.speaker: Mr. G.
sp.p: Yes; Mr. Bounderby has long hoped that the time would arrive when he might, with propriety, offer you his hand in marriage. That time has now arrived; Mr. Bounderby entreats me to make the proposal known to you, and express the hope that you will immediately take it into your favourable consideration.

sp.speaker: Lou.
sp.p: Father, do you think I love Mr. Bounderby?

sp.speaker: Mr. G.
sp.p: Why, my dear, as to that, I really cannot say.

sp.speaker: Lou.
sp.p: Do you ask me to love him?

sp.speaker: Mr. G.
sp.p: No, my dear, no; I ask nothing.

sp.speaker: Lou.
sp.p: Does Mr. Bounderby ask me to love im?

sp.speaker: Mr. G.
sp.p: Really, Louisa, it is difficult to answer your questions,

sp.speaker: Lou.
sp.p: Difficult to answer yes or no, father?

sp.speaker: Mr. G.
sp.p: Louisa, this is no catalogue of questions and answers. It is simply a communication of fact—tangible fact. Now, what are the facts? You are, we will say, in round numbers, twenty years of age. Mr. Bounderby, we will say, in round numbers, is fifty-five—there or thereabouts. This is a slight disparity in your respective years; but in means and position, you are equal. Then the question arises: is a trifling disparity sufficient to operate as a bar to such a marriage? I find, on reference to figures, that a large proportion of marriages are contracted between parties of very unequal ages, and that the elder of the contracting parties is, in rather more than three-fourths of the instances, the bridegroom. It is so among the natives of the British possessions in India; also in a considerable part of China, and among the Calmucks of Tartary; and the best means of computation furnished us by travellers yield similar results.

sp.speaker: Lou.
sp.p: What do you recommend, father?

sp.speaker: Mr. G.
sp.p: A consideration of this one fact. Does Mr. Bounderby ask you to marry him? Yes, he does. The sole remaining question is—will you marry him? Nothing can be plainer.

sp.speaker: Lou.
sp.p: Shall I marry him?

sp.speaker: Mr. G.
sp.p: I leave you to judge for yourself. I have stated the case, as such cases are usually stated among all practical minds. I have stated the case as your mother's case and my case were stated in its time; it is for you to decide. I see, you hesitate; I see
sp.stage: (turns, and beholds Louisa looking out of the window)
sp.p: , you are absolutely looking out of the window at the most critical period of your life—your eventful life! Are you, Miss Louisa, consulting the chimneys of the Coketown works?
What is it you see?

sp.speaker: Lou.
sp.p: There seems to be nothing here but languid and monotonous smoke; yet, when the night comes, fire bursts out.

sp.speaker: Mr. G.
sp.p: What has fire to do with marriage, Louisa?

sp.speaker: Lou.
sp.p: Father, I have often thought that life is very short.

sp.speaker: Mr. G.
sp.p: It is short, my dear—very short; still, the average duration of human life has increased of late years; the calculation of the best actuaries attest the fact.

sp.speaker: Lou.
sp.p: I speak of my own life, father.

sp.speaker: Mr. G.
sp.p: Indeed! yours is governed by the same laws which govern lives in the aggregate.

sp.speaker: Lou.
sp.p: While it lasts, I would wish to do the little I can, and the little I am fit for. What does it matter?

sp.speaker: Mr. G.
sp.p: What matter, my dear?

sp.speaker: Lou.
sp.p: Mr. Bounderby asks me to marry him. The question I have to ask myself is, shall I marry him? That is so, father, is it not?

sp.speaker: Mr. G.
sp.p: Certainly, my dear.

sp.speaker: Lou.
sp.p: Let it be so. Since Mr. Bounderby likes to take me thus, I am satisfied to accept his proposals. Tell him, father, as soon as you can, that this was my answer; repeat it, word for word, because I should wish him to know what I said.

sp.speaker: Mr. G.
sp.p: I will observe your very proper request. Have you any wish in reference to the period of your marriage?

sp.speaker: Lou.
sp.p: None, father; what does it matter?

sp.speaker: Mr. G.
sp.p: Bless me! I had nearly forgotten one very important fact! I ought to ask, and I do ask, if you have ever entertained in secret any other proposal?

sp.speaker: Lou.
sp.p: No, father. Had such been the case, I should not now so suddenly make my election— what have I seen?—whom have I seen? what are my heart's experiences?

sp.speaker: Mr. G.
sp.p: My dear Louisa, you correct me justly. Kiss me, my dear child; and let us communicate the happy tidings to your mother!

div.head: SCENE II.
div.stage: —The parlour at Bounderby's Bank. BITZER in attendance upon MR. SPARSIT.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: All shut up, Bitzer?

sp.speaker: Bit.
sp.p: Yes; all is shut up, ma'am.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: What is the news of the day?—anything of moment?

sp.speaker: Bit.
sp.p: Nothing 'tickler, ma'am. The cat has kittened on the old ledger, ma'am; and—

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: I don't seek intelligence of that sort; my remarks apply to the bipeds, Bitzer, not to the quadrupeds. How about the people?—what are they doing now?

sp.speaker: Bit.
sp.p: Going on the old way, ma'am—uniting and leaguing, and engaging to stand by one another.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: I say, once for all, these strikes are abominable. These people must be conquered. It is high time they were put down.

sp.speaker: Bit.
sp.p: Yes, ma'am; that is exactly what I say myself; you couldn't have put it clearer, nohow.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: Has it been a busy day, Bitzer?

sp.speaker: Bit.
sp.p: Not 'tickler busy, ma'am;—a fair average day.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: The clerks trustworthy, punctual, and industrious, of course?

sp.speaker: Bit.
sp.p: Pretty fair, as times go, with the usual exception.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: Indeed! What exception?

sp.speaker: Lou.
sp.p: Mr. Thomas, ma'am—I doubt Mr. Thomas very much. I don't like his ways—nohow at all.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: Bitzer, you forget my positive injunctions about names.

sp.speaker: Bit.
sp.p: I beg pardon; it is quite true that you did object to names being used at all, and they are always best avoided; but, though I says it, that there Mr. Thomas is—

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: Hush! I do not consider I should be scrupulously true to the interests of my employer if I allowed names to be used under this roof, that are, unfortunately—no doubt, too unfortunately, for him—connected with him.

sp.speaker: Bit.
sp.p: I twig, my lady.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: Say an individual, and I will hear you.

sp.speaker: Bit.
sp.p: Well then, madam, that there individual has never once been what he ought to have been since he first put his foot in the place. That individual is a dissipated; that individual is always a-chalking figures of you and another individual at the back of the office-door, to make a lot of smaller individuals laugh;—that individual is not worth his salt, ma'am. No; he wouldn't get neither, if he hadn't got a friend and relation at Court, ma'am.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: Too true, Bitzer; too true.

sp.speaker: Bit.
sp.p: Yet the individual is to be pitied, ma'am; the individual is as unprovided, and as extravagant an individual as any in town—you know what their improvidence is, ma'am? No one could know it better than a lady of your experience does.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: They should take example by you, Bitzer.

sp.speaker: Bit.
sp.p: Thank you, ma'am; since you refer to me, ma'am, I will speak. Look at me, ma'am! I have put by a little already; I have the gratuity I get at Christmas I never touch; I don't even go to the length of my wages, though they are not much. Why cannot the individual do as I am obliged to do? What one individual can do, surely another individual can do? I am sure, we are constantly hearing about wives and families, until it becomes sickening. Look at me, ma'am! What do I want a with a wife? what could I do with a family? I have only one individual to feed, and that's the individual I do like to feed.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: Right, Bitzer—right!
Heyday! who can want me at this late hour of the night? Go and see directly.
A most improper hour of the day for any one to call at the Bank.

sp.speaker: Bit.
sp.p: An individual, ma'am.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: His name?

sp.speaker: Bit.
sp.p: You told me never to mention names, so I did not ask him; he says, however, he wants you.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: Usher the gentleman in.

sp.speaker: Bit.
sp.p: The individual has ushered himself in, ma'am—for here the individual comes.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: What are your commands, sir, with me?

sp.speaker: Hart.
sp.p: I beg pardon—you will excuse my seeming madness; but if you wish to know whether I wish to speak to you, I certainly seek that superlative pleasure. I left my fellow at the railway-station, looking after my luggage; very heavy train, and vast quantity of it in the van; so strolled on to look about me. Exceedingly odd place, this; dear lady, permit me to ask, if it is always as black as this?

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: In general, much blacker.

sp.speaker: Hart.
sp.p: Dear me, what a very odd place! You are not a native?

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: Oh, dear no, sir! It was once my good fortune—that is to say, before I was a widow— to move in a far different sphere: my husband was a Powler.

sp.speaker: Hart.
sp.p: Beg pardon—a what?—a—

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: A Powler.

sp.speaker: Hart.
sp.p: A fowler—fowl—a shooting-man!

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: A member of the Powler family,

sp.speaker: Hart.
sp.p: Ah, I see; and must say, that so charming a specimen of the Fowler—Powler family, I should say—must be very much bored here.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: I am the servant of circumstances, sir; and I have long adapted myself to the governing power of my life. May I ask to what I am indebted for the honour of this visit?

sp.speaker: Hart.
sp.p: I beg ten thousand pardons. I bear a letter of introduction to Mr.—Mr. Boundabout —a banker, or something of that sort; and walking through this most extraordinary black town, whilst they deviled me a chicken at the hotel, I asked somebody whom I met, and who was all fluffy, and covered up from top to toe with the raw material they make in this place, if he knew where Boundabout lived; and as I asked for the banker, he naturally enough directed me to the Bank; but I now perceive that Mr. Boundabout, the banker, does not reside in the edifice, beneath whose roof I have the honour to offer this explanation.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: No, sir; he does not.

sp.speaker: Hart.
sp.p: I had no intention of delivering my letter; but, observing at the window a lady of a very superior and agreeable appearance, I considered that I could not do better than ask that lady where Mr. Boundabout the banker lives— which, I assuredly venture, with all suitable apologies to do, of course, you know the banker well?

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: Yes, sir. In my dependant situation, I have known him more than twelve years.

sp.speaker: Hart.
sp.p: Quite an interest. I think he has, or will be, married to Mr. Gradgrind's daughter.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: He is to enjoy that honour.

sp.speaker: Hart.
sp.p: And the lady, I hear, is quite a philosopher.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: Is she? Indeed! I was not aware—

sp.speaker: Hart.
sp.p: Excuse my impertinent curiosity; but, as you know the family, and appear to know the world, I would ask, is the lady so very alarming? Her father gives her such a portentously hard-headed reputation that I have a great desire to know her too. Is she so absolutely unapproachable? Repellently and stunningly clever? I see by your meaning smile you think differently. As to age, now? Forty? Not so much? Thirty-five, perhaps?

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: A mere chit, sir. Under twenty.

sp.speaker: Hart.
sp.p: I am astonished! I give you my honour, Mrs. Fow—Mrs. Powler, that I was never more astonished in the whole course of my life. Under twenty! The father's manner prepared me for a grim and stony maturity. I am obliged to you for correcting so absurd a mistake.
You will excuse me for going but—
Under twenty! Is it possible?

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: What do you think of the gentleman, Bitzer?

sp.speaker: Bit.
sp.p: The gentleman spends a deal of money on his dress, ma'am. There's half a year's salary in his coat and trousers; and I don't know how many Christmas-boxes in his boots.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: It must be admitted they are fashionable.

sp.speaker: Bit.
sp.p: Yes, ma'am; if fashion is worth the money. It looks to me, ma'am, as if the individual got them by gaming.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: It is highly immoral to game, Bitzer.

sp.speaker: Bit.
sp.p: Highly ridiculous, ma'am. Besides, the chances are against the individuals themselves. I never play at pitch and toss myself, and I hate going the odd man.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: Oh, you fool! you fool!

div.stage: (Shaking her fist at a portrait of Mr Bounderby, as she goes out.)

div.head: SCENE III.
div.stage: As the Scene opens, the party discovered cheering. GRADGRIND, BOUNDERBY, DR. SOMERFORD, TOM, and all the male guests wear wedding favours; the ladies are in white; the bride in satin. Table elegantly laid out.

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: Ladies and gentlemen, since you have done my wife and myself the honour of drinking our health and happiness, I suppose I must acknowledge the same; though, as you all know me, and know what I am, and what my extraction was, you won't expect a speech from a man who, when he sees a pump, says, “That's a pump;” and when he sees a post, says, “That's a post;” and is not to be got to call a post a pump, or either of them a toothpick.

sp.speaker: Omnes.
sp.p: Hear, hear, hear!

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: If you want a speech this morning, my friend and father-in-law, Tom Gradgrind, is a member of parliament, and you know where to get it. However, if I feel a little independent when I look around this table, and feel how little I thought of marrying Tom Gradgrind's daughter when I was a ragged street-boy, who never washed his face unless it was at a pump, and then only once a fortnight, I hope I may be excused. I hope you will like my being independent; if you don't, I can't help it. I do feel independent. Now, I have mentioned, and you have mentioned, that I am this day married to Tom Gradgrind's daughter. I am very happy to be married to Tom Gradgrind's daughter. It was long my wish to be married to Tom Gradgrind's daughter. I have watched her bringing up, and I believe she is worthy of me.

sp.speaker: Omnes.
sp.p: Hear, hear, hear!

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: At the same time, not to be misunderstood, I believe I'm quite worthy of her.

sp.speaker: Omnes.
sp.p: Hear, hear, hear!

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: I thank you humbly for the good-will you have shown to me; and the best wish I can give the unmarried portion of the company is this—I hope every bachelor may find as good a wife as Tom Gradgrind's daughter, and I hope every spinster may find as good a husband as Tom Gradgrind's daughter has found.

sp.speaker: Omnes.
sp.p: Hear, hear, hear!

div.stage: (In the midst of the cheers, Mr. Harthouse strolls into the apartment. The company rise and leave.)

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: Oh, my dear Mr. Harthouse! I have been most anxiously waiting to see you. You will now allow me to tell you something about our town of Coketown.

sp.speaker: Hart.
sp.p: Shall be most proud and happy.

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: Don't you make too sure of that. First of all, you see, we smoke. That's meat and drink to me. It's healthy in all respects, and particularly so for the lungs. If you are one of those who wish to consume it, I differ with you. We are not going to wear the bottoms of our boilers out any faster than we do for all the humbugging sentiments in Great Britain and Ireland.

sp.speaker: Hart.
sp.p: I'm completely and entirely of your opinion upon conviction.

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: Glad to hear it. Now, you have heard lots about the work in our mills, no doubt. It's the pleasantest work in the world. We couldn't improve the mills if we laid Turkey carpets down, which, of course, we are not going to do. I have now one important thing to say. Now, don't deceive yourself by supposing you are associating with a man of family. I am a bit of dirty riffraff, sir,—a dirty, genuine scrap of tag, rag, and bobtail. We may, therefore, shake hands on easy terms; and I am come to know how you do, and to hope you are pretty well.

sp.speaker: Hart.
sp.p: You are eccentric, Mr. Bounderby; but the founders of great fortunes are eccentric— very eccentric.

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: Perhaps you know, or perhaps you don't know, I mentioned Tom Gradgrind's daughter. If you have nothing better to do, I'll introduce you to Tom Gradgrind's daughter; and, as good luck will have it, here comes Tom Gradgrind's daughter.

sp.speaker: Hari.
sp.p: Mr. Bounderby, you anticipate my wishes.

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: This, sir, is my wife. Louisa, Mr. James Harthouse. Mr. Harthouse has joined your father's muster-roll. If he is not Tom Gradgrind's colleague before long, I believe we shall hear of him in connection with one of our leading towns. You observe, Mr. Harthouse, that my wife is some years my junior. I don't know what she saw in me to marry me; but she saw something in me, I suppose, or she wouldn't have married me. Now, Loo, let's have something in your best style for dinner—some capital soup, if you please, my dear. By Jove! Mr. Harthouse, talking of soup reminds me of my boyish days. I never relished any soup in my life so much as the flavour of the ha'porth of stewed eels I purchased in the streets when I was eight years of age. By the Lord Harry, sir! I think, young as I was, I think I must have eaten three horses in the disguise of polonies and saveloys. Yes, I have; and washed them down with copious draughts of dirty water, as it gushed from the grimy holes of the dust-carts.

sp.speaker: Hart.
sp.p: Ha, ha, ha! How droll! Mr. Bounderby is remarkably facetious with his anecdotes, Mrs. Bounderby.

sp.speaker: Lou.
sp.p: Mr. Bounderby occasionally forgets the presence of his wife, sir. You must pardon his ill-timed reminiscences.

sp.speaker: Hart.
sp.p: Mr. Bounderby is a noble animal in a comparatively natural state, quite free from the harness in which a conventional hack like myself works; but if he has said anything offensive to the ears of his wife, I humbly apologise for him.

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: Stuff! Nonsense! Harthouse, you must not mind. She'll be compelled to hear a great deal worse before we have been married many months. I always said I would not allow my wife to lord it over me; and I'm sure I shall begin with Tom Gradgrind's daughter.
At last, sirrah? When I was your age, I was always punctual, or I got no luncheon.

sp.speaker: Tom.
sp.p: When you were my age, you hadn't a wrong balance to set right, and to drop afterwards.

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: Never mind that now.

sp.speaker: Tom.
sp.p: Well, then, don't you begin with me.

sp.speaker: Hart.
sp.p: Your brother's face is familiar to me. Can I have met him abroad, or at some public school, perhaps?

sp.speaker: Lou.
sp.p: No; he was educated at home. Tom, dear, I was telling Mr. Harthouse that he could not have seen you abroad.

sp.speaker: Tom.
sp.p: No such luck, sir.

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: Well, get your luncheon, and then follow me to the Bank. Come, Loo! Mr. Harthouse, I will be with you in a few minutes. In the meantime, there's champagne, hock, burgundy, claret, madeira, port, or sherry at your service.

sp.speaker: Hart.
sp.p: Come, Tom, give the wine a name.

sp.speaker: Tom.
sp.p: I just will. Champagne, by all means. The governor don't keep the worst in the world.

sp.speaker: Hart.
sp.p: Do you smoke?

sp.speaker: Tom.
sp.p: Does a duck swim?

sp.speaker: Hart.
sp.p: You won't get a better in these parts.

sp.speaker: Tom.
sp.p: For that reason, I mean to enjoy it.

sp.speaker: Hart.
sp.p: Come, Tom—a bumper.

sp.speaker: Tom.
sp.p: Ay; to the brim, and over!
What a jolly, easy swell he is, to be sure!

sp.speaker: Hart.
sp.p: Here's your sister's good health!

sp.speaker: Tom.
sp.p: Thanks. I say, Mr. Harthouse, you have had a dose of old Bounderby, to-day.

sp.speaker: Hart.
sp.p: What a comical brother-in-law you are, to be sure!

sp.speaker: Tom.
sp.p: What a comical brother-in-law, old Bounderby is, I think you mean!

sp.speaker: Hart.
sp.p: You are satirical, Master Tom.

sp.speaker: Tom.
sp.p: Not I; but I don't care for old Bounderby, if you mean that?

sp.speaker: Hart.
sp.p: But his wife—Mrs. Bounderby?

sp.speaker: Tom.
sp.p: Well, she don't care for old Bounderby, either. What! my sister Loo? Not she!

sp.speaker: Hart.
sp.p: In the past tense, you mean. We are in the present tense now.

sp.speaker: Tom.
Hart.
sp.p: Good!
But you don't mean it?

sp.speaker: Tom.
sp.p: But I do mean it, upon my honour. You don't suppose my beautiful sister, Louisa—our Loo—ever cared for old Bounderby, do you?

sp.speaker: Hart.
sp.p: My dear fellow, what am I to suppose, when I find two persons living in completed happiness and harmony together?

sp.speaker: Tom.
sp.p: I wasn't so very much surprised, after all, at Loo's marrying the old gentleman. Loo never had a lover. Father proposed, mother thought it a great catch; and, before Loo knew what she was about, they were spliced.

sp.speaker: Hart.
sp.p: Very dutiful in your interesting sister.

sp.speaker: Tom.
sp.p: But she wouldn't have been so very dutiful if it had not been for me—hic—I gave the casting vote—hic—I persuaded her to accept the old gentleman; and he, in return, popped me into his bank.

sp.speaker: Hart.
sp.p: Clever diplomatist!

sp.speaker: Tom.
sp.p: She's a regular girl; and a girl, you know, can get on anywhere. But Loo's not a common girl; that is to say, not a common sort of girl. She can shut herself up within herself, and think for hours. It's all father's doings; he formed her.

sp.speaker: Hart.
sp.p: I see—made the lady a complete philosopher.

sp.speaker: Tom.
sp.p: And me, too, I'm—hic—a phi—losopher.

sp.speaker: Hart.
sp.p: No, surely!

sp.speaker: Tom.
sp.p: When first I got stuck in old Bounderby's bank, I was as flat as a warming-pan—hic—I knew nothing about life—not a bit. I was as ignorant as an oyster.

sp.speaker: Hart.
sp.p: One glass more.
Come, a joke's a joke; you cannot mean what you say of Mr. Bounderby? You don't appear to have the same reverence or that worthy gentleman which exists in the bosom of Mrs. Sparsit.

sp.speaker: Tom.
sp.p: Mother Sparsit! What!—hic—you have seen that old she-dragon already? She loves Loo—hic—with more than admiration—say, devotion. Mother Sparsit! she never see her cap at old Bounderby; oh, no! Couldn't do it at any price!—hic—I say, how my head swims! Your tobacco is too mild.

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: Tom! Tom Gradgrind!

sp.speaker: Tom.
sp.p: That's him! Call away!—hic—I'll not stir—I'll not budge a foot! I'll be damned if I do!

sp.speaker: Hart.
sp.p: You had better stroll into the garden; it is charmingly cool. In ten minutes, I'll join you. Your brother-in-law may be angry.

sp.speaker: Tom.
sp.p: Who cares for him? What! Joe Bounderby? what, old Joe?
Not I! I'm —hic—an upright man, and care for nobody!

sp.speaker: Hart.
sp.p: Let me persuade you to go.

sp.speaker: Tom.
sp.p: I'll fight him—hic—or any other man— hic—only a one-er in the ribs—You won't?—hic —I'll fight the two—hic. One down, the other come on!

sp.speaker: Hart.
sp.p: Out, out, I say!

sp.speaker: Tom.
sp.p: Loo! dear Loo! Be kind to sister Loo!

sp.speaker: Hart.
sp.p: Yes, yes

kinder, I fear, than Loo is likely to prove to me. But, “faint heart never won fair lady.” So far, so good; like a well-squeezed lemon, Master Thomas, I have no further use for you, and have continently thrown you away; 'pon honour!

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: Now, Stephen, I tell you, once for all, that it is clear to me, that you are one of those chaps that have always got a grievance. You go about sowing it, and raising crops; that's the business of your life, my friend!

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.p: I canna argue wi' you, sir; but I feel it my duty to say, that, unless something be done, and that quickly, you will lose all the hands in Coketown.

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: What the deuce do you complain of?

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.p: I ha' not coom here complaining; I have only come to say that I had a terrible life at factory, what wi' one and what wi' t'other, because I keep aloof from agitation, like.

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: Pooh, pooh! you are such a waspish, rapish, ill-conditioned chap, you are, that even your own union will have nothing to do with you. I never thought these fellows could be right in anything; but I'll tell you what—I'll so far go along with them, for a novelty, that I'll have nothing more to do with you either.

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.p: Be it coom to this? Do I hear right— standing out, as I have done, against all the combination men and their leader? Do I hear right, Mr. Bounderby?

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: Perfectly right. Finish off what you are at, and then go elsewhere.

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.p: Sir, you know—weel, that, if I cannot get work with you, I cannot get it elsewhere.

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: What I know, I know. I know this—I'll have no more to say to you. Your way is in that direction, Mr. Blackpool
—in that direction.

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.p: Heaven help us all! My load was heavy enough, in all conscience; but I must bear up till this poor heart breaks beneath the weight of it.

sp.speaker: Bit.
sp.p: Here's a pretty kettle of fish, in broad daylight! I've just met a certain individual, and he's as drunk as a lord! Rolling about in the garden, he dropped his diary, which I and another individual picked up, and means to keep till there's a reward offered for its restoration. Let me see if he keeps a faithful account of his daily expenditure.

Monday: Twelve dishes of oysters, four plates of deviled kidneys, sixteen “goes” of pale brandy, —that's his dinner. Six anchovy toasts, four plates of muffins, two ditto of crumpets, prawns, collared brawn, water-cresses, and three dishes of broiled ham—a tidy tea. Supper: Three lobsters and shrimp sauce, four glasses of cold punch and sundry “goes” of brandy at the bar of the “Constitution” before going to bed, £2 12s. 6d. Pretty well for one day. Tuesday: Fowl, ham, and cold turkey. Breakfast. Luncheon for six at the Bank. £2 for share in a raffle of a dog-cart, which, of course, the individual did not win. Wednesday: Red-letter day. How did the individual spend his holiday. Let me see. Hired horse and chaise to drive fellow-clerks to the hurdle race, £100s. Supper to said clerks, on coming home with extra large bowl of hot punch and one dozen of champagne, because the individual was a lucky individual, and won a bet of half-a-crown. Another £5, at least. Now, where does the money come from, which is required to square all these extravagances? I must keep a sharp look-out, or the individual may be short in his accounts some fine morning. I'll just consult Mrs. Sparsit about this. Hurdle-race, indeed! I never went to a hurdle-race in my life. I refused to go to the last; and I wouldn't be seen at one for a quarter's salary.

div.head: SCENE IV.
div.stage: Enter RACHEL, at door; goes to table, takes a candle from it, and lights it. She then opens the door, and gives a light to STEPHEN and MRS. PEGLER, who enter.

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.p: Take a seat, missus; you must be main tired.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Yes, I've come forty good mile again to get a sight at the lady. I hear of Mr. Bounderby's getting married. I read it in the papers, where it looked so grand! It looked fine! I want to see his wife, of all things. I have not seen her yet. Now, wasn't it most provoking? If you'll believe me, she never even came to the window, or stirred from the Bank all day. I have been watching there since six o'clock this morning. I saw you come out of the house; and, like a good, communicating angel, you tell me that you have seen her. What is she like?

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.p: I ha' seen the lady—she be young and handsome, wi' fine dark eyes, wi' a still way, Rachel, as I never seed the likes on in a' my loife.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Young and handsome! What a happy wife!

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.p: Well, I suppose she is—she must be.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Certainly, for she's your master's wife, isn't she?

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.p: Why, as to maister, he's no maister of mine onny longer. It's a' ended between him and me.

sp.speaker: Rac.
sp.p: Stephen, you haven't thrown up your work?

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.p: Whether I ha' thrown it up, or it ha' thrown me up, it be a' the same. I ha' now got to begin the world again. I shan't go my ways to-night, nor to-morrow night; but I shall soon; and yet, Rachel, I be more gladsome and leat under it than I could have expected. In the meantime, I will try to look joyfully for the day when we shall walk together, far away in that happy region far above, where feyther, mother, and mouny sisters and brothers are. Now, coom; we mon take a parting cup, too. You'll take a cup too—won't you, missus?

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Yes; and thank you heartily, for I'm sore fatigued, and a dish will fresh me mightily. Would you believe it, I have taken nothing since breakfast.

div.stage: (They sit down to tea, which Rachel has prepared, having taken the things from small cupboard.)

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.p: Now, this look ssnug and comfortable, and makes a man forget a peck of trouble. I ha' not yet thought, missus, of asking you your name.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Pegler. P-E-G—peg—L-E-R—ler— Pegler. I am Deborah Pegler.

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.p: A widow?

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Many long years. The best of husbands lay dead before you were born.

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.p: Onny children? Bless 'em, they garland life.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Don't speak of them now—not now— not now.

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.p: Eh, missus—gone wrong?

sp.speaker: Rac.
sp.p: Dead, Stephen—perhaps dead.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: I had a son, and he did well—ay, wonderfully well; but he is not to be spoken of now, if you please. I have lost him.

div.stage: (Bitzer puts his head in at the door and shouts “Mrs. Bounderby.” Mrs. Pegler starts up, in great alarm.)

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Bounderby! Oh, hide me, hide me! Don't let me be seen—for the world, don't let him get in till I get out, for the wealth of India. Pray, pray don't.

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.p: Don't be frightened, missus. 'Taint Mr. Bounderby, it be his lady that condescends to visit my humble home. She is at the door.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Then pray don't take any notice of me. Don't speak to me, if you please. I'll just get behind this curtain, and be as still as a mouse.

div.stage: (Louisa and Tom are lighted in by Rachel.)

sp.speaker: Lou.
sp.p: I have come, Mr. Blackpool, to speak to you in consequence of what has passed at home just now. I should like to be of service to you, if you will let me. I make no doubt that Stephen has told you what has passed between my husband and himself. You would be his first resource, I think.

sp.speaker: Rac.
sp.p: I have heard the end of it, young lady, and regret it on Stephen's part.

sp.speaker: Lou.
sp.p: Do I understand that, being rejected by one employer, he would probably be rejected by all? I thought he said as much. How comes all this trouble about?

sp.speaker: Rac.
sp.p: He fell into suspicion with all his fellow-workmen, because he had given his promise not to combine against his master.

sp.speaker: Lou.
sp.p: May I ask why he made that promise?

sp.speaker: Rac.
sp.p: I did not seek it of him, lady, but he gave that promise to me; for I made him give his word to avoid trouble for his own good, little thinking that he would come to it through me. But I know he'll die a thousand deaths before he'll break his word.

sp.speaker: Lou.
sp.p: Forgive me, lady, but I must now say a few words—onny a few. No one, excepting myself, can ever know what love and respect I bear to Rachel, or what's the cause. When I gave that promise, I meant to keep it. I tow'd her true, she is the angel of my life, and the promise is recorded there.

sp.speaker: Lou.
sp.p: What do you intend to do? Where to go?

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.p: When I have finished off my work, I shall quit this place, and try another.

sp.speaker: Lou.
sp.p: How will you travel?

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.p: On foot, my lady—on foot.

sp.speaker: Lou.
sp.p: Rachel, will you tell him—for you know how to do so without offence—that this bank-note is given to him to help him on his journey. Beg of him to accept it from me.

sp.speaker: Rac.
sp.p: I cannot do that, young lady. I bless you for thinking of poor Stephen with such tenderness; but 'tis for him to know best what he should do under the circumstances.

sp.speaker: Lon.
sp.p: Well, then, Mr. Blackpool—

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.p: Not even Rachel could by onny words make such a kind offer kinder. To show that I am not a man without reason and gratitude, I'll just tak' two pound. I'll borrow it of you, young lady, to be sure to pay it back again; and it will be the sweetest bit of work that ever I did in my life, that shall find it in my power to return it to you.

sp.speaker: Lou.
sp.p: At any future period, you will know where to find a friend.

sp.speaker: Tom.
sp.p: Just wait a minute, Loo, will you? Before we go, I should like to say a word.
I say, my boy

, I verily believe I can do you a good turn. Don't ask me what it is, because it may not come to anything. I sent our clerk, Bitzer, for you to come to the Bank, but he missed you. Now, when are you going to start?

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.p: Tuesday or Saturday, nigh about.

sp.speaker: Tom.
sp.p: Well, come at night, about ten or eleven o'clock, to the Bank; before you go away, and when I can send to bring you in, I will. Wait for a couple of hours, or so; I sha'n't send for you, unless I find I can do you the service I want to do you. Now, don't you forget, but keep it dark.
Halloa, you! Loo! why don't you wait for me?

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Oh, dear me! How glad I am they are gone! What a sweet young creature she is, to be sure! How very beautiful! What an angelic face, and what a delicate white hand! Just like my hand, at her age. I could have kissed it, if I dared! Now, having seen the lady, and, as it's getting late, and I've four good miles to walk, I had better brush. I am to call for my parcel at the “Traveller's” coffee-shop.

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.p: All in my way. I'll see you safe, if agreeable.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Agreeable! Delightful! Thank you, too.

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.p: I shall see thee again, Rachel, before I go.

sp.speaker: Rac.
sp.p: If not, you will write to me and tell me all that happens; won't you, Stephen?

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.p: That I will. Heaven bless thee! That I will.

div.stage: (Lights them out, closes the door, and follows.)

div.head: SCENE V.

sp.speaker: Hart.
sp.p: Take Godolphir to the stable. I'll stroll across the lawn to the lodge; and harkye, sirrah, if that horrible old woman asks any more questions about me or my business, take her to the nearest horse-pond, and give her a ducking. Thus it is to be bored in the country.

div.stage: BOUNDERBY rushes on, and nearly upsets Harthouse.

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: Harthouse! Harthouse, have you heard?

sp.speaker: Hart.
sp.p: Heard what?

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: Then you have not heard.

sp.speaker: Hart.
sp.p: I have heard, and felt, too. I declare, you have knocked every bit of wind out of my body.

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: The Bank, sir—my Bank!

sp.speaker: Hart.
sp.p: What! has it stopped?

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: No, sir—it's robbed! The Bank is robbed!

sp.speaker: Hart.
sp.p: You don't mean it?

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: Robbed last night, sir—robbed in a most mysterious manner—robbed with a false key!

sp.speaker: Hart.
sp.p: Of much?

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: No—not of much; but it might have been!

sp.speaker: Hart.
sp.p: Of how much?

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: Oh, of a sum, if you stick to a sum, of not more than a hundred and fifty pounds.

sp.speaker: Hart.
sp.p: A trifle.

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: Yes; but it's not the sum, it's the fact of the bank Being robbed. That's the important circumstance. I am quite surprised that you do not see it.

sp.speaker: Hart.
sp.p: I do not see it; and congratulate you, with all my soul, upon its being such a mere fleabite.

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: It might have been twenty thousand pounds.

sp.speaker: Hart.
sp.p: I suppose it might.

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: Suppose it might! By Jupiter, you may suppose so; it might have been twice twenty— there is no knowing what it might have been, only the fellows were disturbed. Here comes Tom Gradgrind's daughter; she knows well what it might have been, though you don't.

div.stage: Enter MR. BOUNDERBY, MRS. SPARSIT and BITZER.

sp.speaker: Hart.
sp.p: How the deuce was this extraordinary robbery accomplished—how was it effected?

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: I'll tell you. You know this lady
—she is a lady, a bred and born lady,—you know Mrs. Sparsit.

sp.speaker: Hart.
sp.p: I have already had the honour—

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: And this young man—you saw him, too, on the same occasion?—very well. They live at the Bank. Well, yesterday afternoon, at the close of business hours, everything was put away as usual in the iron-room, at the outside of which this young man sleeps, to guard it; there was—never mind how much in the little safe in young Tom's closet, the safe used for petty cash—there was therein deposited one hundred and fifty odd pounds—

sp.speaker: Bit.
sp.p: One hundred and fifty four—seven—one—

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: Come, let me have none of your interruptions. It's quite enough to be robbed, while you are snoring, because you are too comfortable, without being put right by your four—seven— one. I didn't snore myself when I was your age, let me tell you. I never had victuals enough to snore; and I didn't four—seven—one it,—not if I knew it.

sp.speaker: Bit.
sp.p: I beg pardon, sir; but every individual ought to be correct where money is concerned.

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: Hold your tongue, sir. It was a hundred and fifty odd pound, sir. That sum of money our young Tom locked up in his safe, not a very strong safe, you'll say; but that's no matter now everything was left all right. Some time in the night, whilst this young fellow snored—Mrs. Sparsit, ma'am, you say you have repeatedly heard him snore?

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: Sir, I cannot say that I have heard him precisely snore, and cannot conscientiously make that statement; but, on winter nights, when he has fallen asleep at his table, I have heard him, what I should prefer to describe as partially choke. I have certainly heard him, on such occasions, produce sounds of a nature similar to what may be heard in Dutch clocks; not that I would convey any imputation on his moral character—far from that; I have always considered him a young man of upright principles, and to that I cheerfully give my testimony.

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: Well, while he was snoring, or choking, or, Dutch clocking, or something or other' some fellows—whether previously concealed in the house or not remains to be seen—got to young Tom's safe, forced it, and abstracted the contents; being then disturbed, they made off, letting themselves out at the main; and double locking it afterwards (it was double locked, and this key under the lady's pillar) with a false key, which was picked up in a street near the Bank, about twelve o'clock to-day; no alarm takes place till this morning, when this snoring, choking, Dutch-clocking chap, turns out of bed, and prepares for business; then, looking at Tom's safe, he sees the door ajar, and finds the lock forced, and the money gone.

sp.speaker: Hart.
sp.p: Where is Master Thomas?

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: Staying at the Bank, and helping the police. I wish these fellows had tried to rob me at his time of life; they would have been out of pocket, if they had only invested sixpence in the job, I can tell them that.

sp.speaker: Hart.
sp.p: Anybody suspected?

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: I should say there was, indeed! There's a whole gang of them, and my eye is on the principal. What should you say if I told you that one of my own hands did the deed?

sp.speaker: Hart.
sp.p: Not our friend Blackpot, I hope?

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: Say Pool, instead of Pot, sir, and you have hit the man. I publicly accuse Stephen Blackpool of the robbery!

sp.speaker: Omnes.
sp.p: Stephen Blackpool!

div.head: SCENE I.
div.stage: MR. BOUNDERBY and MRS. SPARSIT discovered.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: Pray, sir, if I may venture to ask, have you received any intelligence respecting the late bare-faced robbery?

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: Not yet, not yet; I don't expect it just yet. Rome was not built in a day.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: True, sir.

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: If Romulus and Remus could wait, Josiah Bounderby can wait—they were better off in their youth than I was, howe'er, they had a she-wolf for a nurse. I had only a she-wolf for a grandmother; she didn't give me any milk, ma'am, she only gave me kicks and bruises—she was a regular Alderney at that. My injunction is, to keep all quiet, and let it blow over. Do what you like under the rose, but don't let anybody know what you are about, or they'll get the fellow who has bolted out of the way.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: But that mysterious old woman in the red cloak still hovers about the Bank—is she taken?

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: She is not yet laid hold of; but she will, she may take her oath of that, if that is any satisfaction to her villanous old mind. I am going into the country on important business for a day or two; you can run down to my house and stay home there till I come.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: Mr. Bounderby, your will is law to me. I go upon your invitation; but I have a strong forboding that my visit will not be agreeable to Miss Gradgrind—Mrs. Louisa Bounderby, I mean.

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: When I invite you to my house, madam, I should hope you want no other invitation.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: Say no more, sir, I shall go with pleasure; but pray take care of yourself for my—for your own sake—for all our sakes.

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: Mum. Not a word to anybody. I'm up to a dodge of my own, and mean in the long run to spring a mine.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: I insist upon tying this warm comforter round your neck, and I will insist upon seeing you put this pocket-pistol into your great-coat-pocket; it contains the smallest drop in the world of your favourite cordial.

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: I thank you, Mrs. Sparsit—I do, indeed.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: And if I might so far presume, I would extort a promise of one line—only one line—to inform me of your safe arrival. I shall be quite low-spirited and uneasy, till you return. Pray, pray, be careful.
I would not, for worlds, that anything should happen to such a good, kind, generous

, silly, egregious, old ass! So, so, Madame Bounderby, I have a chance of hurling you from your high estate. Your foot is on the first step of the ladder leading to your destruction; and all your art of cunning shall never blind me. Bitzer!

sp.speaker: Bit.
sp.p: How is that humble individual, ever obedient to your call?

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: Present my compliments to—you know who—when you go—you know where—and say— he knows who—will be very happy to see him, to partake of he knows what.

sp.speaker: Bit.
sp.p: The individual knows what to come for, and when to come. He's an individual, Dr. Faustus, for here he comes.

sp.speaker: Tom.
sp.p: Delicious! I nosed it on the stairs. I could have sworn those chops were cooked.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: Slightly wrong, Mr. Thomas; they were cooked for dear Mr. Bounderby; but the dear good creature had really no time to partake of them, and he said I might give them to the clerks; and you being the youngest—

sp.speaker: Tom.
sp.p: By Jove! at this kind of work, I am not not to be outdone by the eldest.

div.stage: (Eats rapidly at the table, by which he seats himself.)

sp.speaker: Bit.
sp.p: Some individuals say grace before meat, other individuals are graceless altogether, and act disgracefully.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: How is Mr. Harthouse, sir?

sp.speaker: Tom.
sp.p: Tol, lol! He's all right.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: Where may he be at present?

sp.speaker: Tom.
sp.p: Out shooting. He sent Loo a basket of game as big as a church, yesterday. More chops, please, ma'am.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: How kind! I was sure he was a good shot. He knows how to bag his game.

sp.speaker: Tom.
sp.p: Crack-shot. Pale ale, if you please.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: Mr. Harthouse is a great favourite of mine. We may expect the pleasure of seeing him again shortly.

sp.speaker: Tom.
sp.p: To-morrow, please the pigs, I shall see him to-morrow—more Alsopp, if you please, ma'am
sp.stage: (keeps continually pouring out the pale ale)
sp.p: —he stops at sister's over Sunday, and says he'll lend me his dog and his gun, if I like to go out shooting a bit.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: Indeed!

sp.speaker: Tom.
sp.p: Any more chops, ma'am?

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: By the way, will you remember a message to your sister, for me?

sp.speaker: Tom.
sp.p: I'll try if it's not quite so long as your chops are, in coming.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: Merely my respectful compliments; and I fear I shall not be able to trouble her with my society this week, being still very nervous.

sp.speaker: Tom.
sp.p: If that's all, it won't matter if I forget it. Loo won't think of you if she don't see you. Any more chops?

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: The chops, I am sorry to say, sir—

sp.speaker: Tom.
sp.p: Don't make any apology. I've cleared the decks, and now I'm off.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: The brute! But I have wormed it out of him. So, so! he's to have the dog and gun, and so be sent out of the way; whilst he is away, I'll watch them, even as a cat watches the mice, Bitzer!

sp.speaker: Bit.
sp.p: Here, ma'am.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: What sort of a night is it?

sp.speaker: Bit.
sp.p: It's a soaker, ma'am; and any individual who ventures out will get wet through.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: In such a cause, what matters—hail, rain, or snow? Umbrella, Bitzer!

sp.speaker: Bit.
sp.p: Yes, ma'am. Anything else, ma'am?

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: Clogs.

sp.speaker: Bit.
sp.p: Yes, ma'am.
Some individuals, I think, are cracked.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: I'll be down upon them when they least expect it. Where is the man—let alone the woman —could elude my vigilance, I should like to know?

sp.speaker: Bit.
sp.p: The individual below has borrowed your umbrella, ma'am; but here's mine, if it's of any use.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: Pshaw! I shall take a first-class ticket. When Mrs. Sparsit condescends to visit, she visits as she ought to do—like what she is, a bred and born lady.

sp.speaker: Bit.
sp.p: What a long tail our individual cat has got, when the old dog is out of her way!

div.head: SCENE II.
div.stage: —A splendid Garden, attached to Mr. Bounderby's.

sp.speaker: Mr. Hart.
sp.p: Mrs. Bounderby, I esteem it a most fortunate circumstance, that I find you alone. I have for some time had a particular wish to speak to you. Your brother, my young friend Tom—there, now, don't blush!—yet, I never, in the whole course of my life, saw anything so captivating as the tinge which now gilds those cheeks.

sp.speaker: Lou.
sp.p: Mr. Harthouse, sir?

sp.speaker: Hart.
sp.p: There, don't frown, though I deserve it; I am a worthless dog, as you will find, except that I am not false. But I have taken a great interest in your brother.

sp.speaker: Lou.
sp.p: Have you an interest in anything, Mr. Harthouse?

sp.speaker: Hart.
sp.p: If you had asked me that question when I first arrived here, I should have said “No;” but, gazing upon those features, I must say, “Yes.”

sp.speaker: Lou.
sp.p: I thank you for any interest you may take in my brother's welfare.

sp.speaker: Hart.
sp.p: I regret to see him so heedless, thoughtless, and extravagant. These qualifications, I fear, must have got him into difficulties.

sp.speaker: Lou.
sp.p: I fear, greatly so.

sp.speaker: Hart.
sp.p: I will be frank. Do you think he games?

sp.speaker: Lou.
sp.p: I have heard him talk of bets, which I think is a kind of gambling.

sp.speaker: Hart.
sp.p: And when he bets, of course, he loses.

sp.speaker: Lou.
sp.p: Too frequently.

sp.speaker: Hart.
sp.p: And when he is called upon to pay, you cannot supply him with money to discharge his miscalled debts of honour.

sp.speaker: Lou.
sp.p: There are secrets which ought to be buried in a sister's bosom when they compromise a brother's integrity; you really have no right to ask such questions, sir; and I beg you will not.

sp.speaker: Hart.
sp.p: You must acquit me of impertinent curiosity; but I really think poor Tom is in trouble, and I wish to lend a helping hand to get him out of it. I cannot shut my eyes to the fact, that the young prodigal has begged or borrowed a very considerable sum from you.

sp.speaker: Lou.
sp.p: You will understand, Mr. Harthouse, that if I say yes, it is not by way of complaint or regret. I would never complain of anything; and what I have done, I do not in the least regret. When I married, I found that my brother was even at that time heavily in debt—heavily, for him. Heavily enough, to oblige me to sell some trinkets. They were no sacrifice; I sold them willingly. Since then, I have given my brother at various times, what money I could spare. I do not know that I have suffered by the act; but, lately, he wanted so large a sum as one hundred pounds in one amount. I was quite unable to give it him, and I have certainly felt uneasy for the consequences. I have kept his secret till now, when, perhaps, I very foolishly entrust it to your honour.

sp.speaker: Hart.
sp.p: In which repository, dear Loo—I mean, dear Mrs. Bounderby,—in which repository it will remain perfectly safe. As to Tom, I have made up my mind to make him as gay as a lark. I like the fellow, and shall discharge all his debts at once.

sp.speaker: Lou.
sp.p: Oh, how good! oh, how kind!—how disinterested of you! And do you really mean to do such a good action? What! on the instant, without security or interest? How good! how generous!

sp.speaker: Hart.
sp.p: No; I am sordid—I am selfish. I must get his beautiful sister to take the trouble off my hands, and pay these filthy creditors in person— of course, out of the money I shall advance for that purpose.

sp.speaker: Lou.
sp.p: I shall be delighted, good, kind creature!

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: Good, kind. Step the second.

sp.speaker: Hart.
sp.p: You will be good enough to meet me at the Bank, for this purpose, to-morrow morning, precisely at eleven to recieve the money.

sp.speaker: Lou.
sp.p: I will be punctual, to the minute.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: Punctual. Step the third. An appointment! I have heard enough.

sp.speaker: Lou.
sp.p: Oh, Mr. Harthouse, how happy your generosity has made me! I am sure that—

sp.speaker: Hart.
sp.p: That you would not refuse me a favour, a very slight favour, if I were to ask it.

sp.speaker: Lou.
sp.p: No; you have a right to demand it.

sp.speaker: Hart.
sp.p: Will you let me have your society for a little while?

sp.speaker: Lou.
sp.p: Yes, certainly; but not here, Mr. Harthouse.

sp.speaker: Hart.
sp.p: But where else? I have so little time to make so much of, and I have come so far, and am so devoted, and so distracted.

sp.speaker: Lou.
sp.p: Mr. Harthouse!

sp.speaker: Hart.
sp.p: So over head-and-heels in love. There never was a slave at once devoted and ill-used by his mistress. To look for her sunny welcome, and to be received in this cold, frigid manner, is heartrending.

sp.speaker: Lou.
sp.p: Am I to say again that I must be left to myself? Elsewhere, sir!

sp.speaker: Hart.
sp.p: But we must meet—we will meet—where shall we meet, my angel?

sp.speaker: Lou.
sp.p: Do we not meet at the Bank, at eleven tomorrow, punctually.

sp.speaker: Hart.
sp.p: Ay—oh, yes; but, you see, that's not exactly the sort of meeting I mean, my dearest, dearest Louisa!

sp.speaker: Lou.
sp.p: Let go my hand, this instant, sir!

sp.speaker: Hart.
sp.p: Your cruel commands must be obeyed implicitly; but if I release your hand, my sweetest Louisa, it must be only to salute those beautiful lips.

div.stage: (Offers to kiss, but is spurned indignantly.)

sp.speaker: Lou.
sp.p: Mr. Harthouse, I now see your drift; and behold unmasked the villain in whom I have reposed my confidence; hence, detested, loathed wretch; and when next you seek to pollute the lips of a virtuous woman, profit by the lesson given to you by Louisa Bounderby!

sp.speaker: Hart.
sp.p: I am in a quandary—rather, a pretty particular sort of mess. I've gone rather too far, I think. There's no retracing my unlucky steps. If that cold and insensible column of marble goes to her horrible husband, I must have serious thoughts of making my will. If the bear has the least spark of revenge in his capacious composition, he'll blow my brains out; or, if I have the luck to wing him, I shall have that abominable whelp, her brother, down upon me; and he is so madly fond of his sister, I should not be surprised if he was to murder me in cold blood. I am wound up, and put bye. I have for years been longing to see the Pyramids of Egypt. Egad! I'll gratify my curiosity, and turn my back upon danger. So, here goes.

“Dear Jack,—It's all up at Coketown —bored out with the place. I'm going in for camels.—Yours affectionately, .” Hem! I'll drop that into the box as I pass the post-office; and if ever they catch me in this dismal town, either for business or pleasure, love or money, may I be—most vulgarly anathematized.

sp.speaker: Bit.
sp.p: I'm certain the individual's he. Whenever I go into that ere individuals room, he starts and turns pale, and cries out, “Who's there?” He just now held a shot-revolver to my face; and if I had not bobbed my head out of the way, I shouldn't have been now on my road to tell Mrs. Sparsit my dreadful suspicions. The individual always said he would go the entire animal, and I'm blessed if he hasn't!

div.head: SCENE III.
div.stage: —Mr. Gradgrind's parlour at night.— MR. GRADGRIND writing at a small desk or table.

sp.speaker: Mr. G.
sp.p: Louisa!

sp.speaker: Lou.
sp.p: Father, I wish to speak to you.

sp.speaker: Mr. G.
sp.p: Louisa! you here, and exposed to such a storm? You alarm, me child.
Louisa, tell me as quickly as you can, what is the matter?

sp.speaker: Lou.
sp.p: Father, you have trained me from my cradle. Father, I curse the hour that I was born to such a destiny. How could you give me life, and take away all the inappreicable things that raise from the state of conscious death? Where are the graces of my soul? What have you done with the garden which should have bloomed here, in this wilderness, miscalled a bosom? If it had ever been here, its ashes would save me from the void in which my whole life sinks! Father, you recollect the last time we conversed in this room?

sp.speaker: Mr. G.
sp.p: Well, Louisa, well?

sp.speaker: Lou.
sp.p: What has risen to my lips now would have risen to my lips then, if you had given me a moment's help.
