Father! if you had known that there had lingered in my breast sensibilities, affections, weaknesses, capable of being cherished into strength, defying all the calculations ever made by man, and no more known to his arithmetic than his Creator is—would you have given me to the husband I now come to tell you I hate?

sp.speaker: Mr. G.
sp.p: No, my child!

sp.speaker: Lou.
sp.p: Yet, father, if I had been stone blind, and I had groped my way by the mere sense of touch, I should have been a million times wiser, happier, more loving and contented, more innocent and human in all respects than I am now, with the eyes I have. Now hear what I have come to say.

sp.speaker: Mr. G.
sp.p: I never knew that you were unhappy, my child. Proceed.

sp.speaker: Lou.
sp.p: But I was, father; and in this condition you proposed my husband to me. I took him. I never made a pretence to him or you that I loved him. I knew, and, father, you knew, and he knew that I never did. I do not reproach you, father— I make no complaint; I am here with another intent. Father, another being other than my husband, whom chance threw in my way, has avowed a passion for your child, and declares his passion for me.

sp.speaker: Mr. G.
sp.p: How, Louisa!

sp.speaker: Lou.
sp.p: I will not tell you his plea for obtaining my confidence—it matters little how he gained it. Father! he did gain it. What you know of the story of my marriage, he soon knew just as well. He knew I looked with horror and contempt upon the husband you have thrust upon me, and he found a pliant hour to pour his venom poison in my ear.

sp.speaker: Mr. S.
sp.p: Louisa, Louisa!

sp.speaker: Lou.
sp.p: I have done no worse than listen to him, father. I have not disgraced my husband; I have not disgraced you.

sp.speaker: Mr. G.
sp.p: My child, my child!

sp.speaker: Lou.
sp.p: This night, my husband being away, he declared himself my lover. He haunts me, and will still haunt me, I fear. Your philosophy and your teaching will not save me. Now, father, you have brought me to this; save me by some other means.

sp.speaker: Mr. G.
sp.p: I will, my child; I will.

sp.speaker: Lou.
sp.p: Do, or I shall fall and die upon the ground here before your very feet.

sp.speaker: Mr. G.
sp.p: No, no, my child—We are interrupted. Come with me into the library.
I would give worlds to annul this cursed and fatal marriage.

div.stage: [Exeunt Gradgrind and Louisa as Mr. Sparsit enters, very wet and muddy.

sp.speaker: Mr. S.
sp.p: How I have suffered in pursuit of this bad and wicked woman. Though I missed her in the train, I am fully prepared to swear that they have gone off together. What have I not endured on behalf of Mr. Bounderby and poor dear Mr. Gradgrind? My white stockings are perfectly green; prickly, nasty things are in my shoes; caterpillars are swarming all over my dress; cold rills are running down my back; I have torn my very best satin dress to pieces, and I have lost my purse in the railway carriage. Never mind! Dear, good Mr. Gradgrind is sure to make me ample amends for detecting the wickedness of his daughter. Oh, here he comes!

sp.speaker: Mr. G.
sp.p: Bless me, Mrs. Sparsit! What brings you here at this time of night?

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: You may well ask that. I am here, as you see. Now, Mr. Gradgrind, compose yourself, and prepare to hear a tale of woe.

sp.speaker: Mr. G.
sp.p: I am in little mood to do so, having heard one in part already.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: It is with feelings of deep commiseration —I may say, pain—that I divulge it, but your daughter Louisa—

sp.speaker: Mr. G.
sp.p: What of her?

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: Is bringing your gray hairs with sorrow to the grave.

sp.speaker: Mr. G.
sp.p: I do not understand you. Speak a little plainer, if you please.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: Louisa, I say, has eloped, left her husband, snapped her fingers at you, and gone off with a parliament-man.

sp.speaker: Mr. G.
sp.p: Indeed!

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: I saw them get into a post-chaise together, and I believe they are off to France or America. Ungrateful girl, to leave so good a father!
I fear I have caught my death of cold, watching the misguided girl in the rain.

sp.speaker: Mr. G.
sp.p: Mrs. Sparsit, madam, as a friend of the family, why did you not attempt to stop them?

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: Oh, I did, Mr. Gradgrind, I did; but the unhappy woman told me to mind my own business; and her guilty paramour—that lavender-scented parliament fellow—threatened to kill me if I gave the alarm. I must apply leeches to the place on my throat where he nearly throttled me.

sp.speaker: Mr. G.
sp.p: You are sure my daughter has gone off?

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: Yes. I'll take my affidavit of that be fore any justice in the county. You are a magistrate yourself. Swear me at once. She's now a-hundred miles away at least. Mr. Gradgrind, my heart bleeds for you. I sincerely pity you.

sp.speaker: Mr. G.
sp.p: Mrs. Sparsit, madam, I don't want pity; I want facts. Never mind your pity, madam. My whole life has been devoted to facts. Now, I am of opinion that every syllable you have been uttering is at variance with the strict principles of fact—in fact, nothing but lies from beginning to end. Do you see that door, madam?

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: Yes, I see the door well enough—the Powler family had just such another. Am I to infer, from your pointing in that direction, that you wish me to leave?

sp.speaker: Mr. G.
sp.p: I do.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: Here's ingratitude. I have sat in my wet clothes for more than three hours. I have caught my death of cold
, and you coolly wish me to return to-night.

sp.speaker: Mr. G.
sp.p: I do.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: As you please, Mr. Gradgrind; but, having lost my purse, you will have to lend me the price of a first-class ticket.

sp.speaker: Mr. G.
sp.p: I shall do no such thing

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: You object to a first-class as being extravagant in one of my dependant character. Well, I must put up with a second.

sp.speaker: Mr. G.
sp.p: I object to any.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: I cannot go in a third class, exposed to the open air, such a night as this.

sp.speaker: Mr. G.
sp.p: Mrs. Sparsit, madam, as you came, so you may go back—walk, crawl, creep, or run; I care not; but, begone you must.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: Will you lend me five shillings?

sp.speaker: Mr. G.
sp.p: William! Thomas!

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: It's of no use your asking them. I have done it already.

sp.speaker: Mr. G.
Mrs. S.
sp.p: This to me? Put a Powler under a pump? Here's a return for all the kindness I have showered upon this ungrateful family! Mr. Gradgrind, I will speak, and don't care who hears it. Flesh and blood cannot bear it. If Mr. Bounderby —dear Mr. Bounderby—doesn't make you shake in your shoes for this, I never was a Powler.

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.p: If you please, sir, Mr. Bounderby, and Master Thomas, and a young woman are below, and they want to see you, sir.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: I should think they did, indeed. Now, Mr. Gradgrind, I shall insist upon a most abject apology from you.

div.stage: Enter MR. BOUNDERBY, in a rage, followed by TOM GRADGRIND.

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: Now, you Tom Gradgrind, I am come here about something which has almost struck me dumb.

sp.speaker: Mr. G.
sp.p: Mr. Josiah Bounderby, I shall write to you a letter.

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: Letter! Letters be --- The present is no time to talk to me about letters. No man shall take a liberty of this kind. No man shall dare to talk to me about letters with my mind in the state it is at present.

sp.speaker: Mr. G.
sp.p: Mr. Bounderby, I speak to you of a special letter. I shall write to you about Louisa.

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: Tom Gradgrind, I speak to you of a very special message. I sent to you in reference to Louisa.
Mrs. Sparsit, ma'am, come forth.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: Oh, Mr. Bounderby, if you did but know! After such abominable treatment, such unmanly, not to say ruffianly, treatment. I have—have—

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: If you cannot get it out, ma'am, allow me o get it out for you. This is not a time for a lady, however highly connected, to be totally inaudible, and seemingly swallowing marbles. Tom Gradgrind, this lady—who is a bred and born lady, tells me she has detected pretty goings on between your daughter and your precious rascally friend, Mr. James Harthouse.

sp.speaker: Mr. G.
sp.p: Indeed!

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: Ay, indeed, and indeed! I am given to understand that she has watched.

sp.speaker: Mr. G.
sp.p: You need not repeat what she has watched. I already know what has passed.

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: You do? Then, perhaps, Mr. Conjuror, you will be so obliging as to put on your magic cap, and tell me where my wife is at this present time.

sp.speaker: Mr. G.
sp.p: Undoubtedly. She is here.

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: Here?

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: Here? Mrs. Bounderby here?

sp.speaker: Mr. G.
sp.p: Restrain these outbreaks, Mr. Bounderby. Louisa is here.
sp.stage: (Tom goes up stage, and drops down.)
sp.p: Let me entreat you, for your sake and her sake, to be more quiet.

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: Mr. Sparsit, if I can restrain my ungovernable rage, I insist upon knowing what apology you have to offer for running about the country, in the dead of night, at express-train pace, with no other luggage than a cock-and-a-bull story?

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: A what, sir? Consider my delicacy!

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: Oh, damn your delicacy, ma'am! What apology have you to offer?

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: Mr. Bounderby, sir, my nerves are at present too much shaken for me to say much, and my health has been too much impaired in your service to admit of my doing anything more to-night than to take refuge in a flood of tears. I—

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: Yes, ma'am, there is something else you may take refuge in; namely, a coach. The coach in which we all came here in is at the door. You will, perhaps, allow me to hand you down to it, and pack you off to the Bank. You have, in your over-zeal to serve me, made a most serious mistake. However, I pardon that, and advise you to get home as fast as you can, put your feet into hot water, take a glass or two of scalding rum and butter in bed, and sleep between the blankets.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: Rum and butter for a Powler! Horrible—

sp.speaker: Tom.
sp.p: A pretty kettle of fish, father, isn't it?

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: Now, Tom Gradgrind, one word to my wife in your presence.

sp.speaker: Mr. G.
sp.p: She is here.

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: Mrs. Bounderby, I don't disturb you, I hope? This is rather an unseasonable hour; but here is a young woman who has been making statements which render my visit necessary here to-night. Gradgrind, as your Tom refuses, for some obstinate reason or other, to say anything at all about these statements, I am obliged to confront her with your daughter. Come forth, young woman.
Now, say your say.

sp.speaker: Rac.
sp.p: You have seen me before, young lady.
You will not, I am sure, deny it?

sp.speaker: Lou.
sp.p: I remember I have.

sp.speaker: Rac.
sp.p: Will you kindly state when, where, and who was present?

sp.speaker: Lou.
sp.p: Oh, certainly. I went to Blackpool's on the night of his discharge from the service of my husband, and I met you there; an elderly female was there also, who did not speak. My brother Tom was with me.

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: Why did you not say so, sir?

sp.speaker: Tom.
sp.p: I promised Loo I wouldn't; and I hate mischief, I do.

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: What, madam, took you? What did you go to that man's house for?

sp.speaker: Lou.
sp.p: I felt compassion for the poor fellow. I went to give him some trifling assistance.

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: Thank you, madam; I am much flattered and obliged.

sp.speaker: Rac.
sp.p: You offered him a bank-note?

sp.speaker: Lou.
sp.p: I did; but the honest fellow would only take two pounds in gold.

sp.speaker: Rac.
sp.p: You hear, sir?

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: Oh, certainly; if you put the question whether such a ridiculous and improbable account is true or not, I am bound to say it is confirmed.

sp.speaker: Rac.
sp.p: Lady, Stephen Blackpool is now named as a thief in public print all over this town, and I don't know where else. There has been a meeting to-night, where he has been spoken of in the most shameful way. Stephen! the honestest lad, the truest lad—the best lad in the whole country!

sp.speaker: Lou.
sp.p: I am sorry, very sorry!

sp.speaker: Rac.
sp.p: I hope you may be, young lady; but I don't know. The like of quality don't care for us poor folk—don't belong to us—don't know us. I cannot say what brought you to our humble abode; but, if it was for evil, and to bring shame upon the poor lad, I am in amaze—I said then, and I repeat it now—you took pitifully to him; but I don't know—I don't know.

sp.speaker: Tom.
sp.p: You're a pretty artiste to come here with your precious imputations! You ought to be bundled out for not knowing how to conduct yourself—and you should be, if I had my way!

sp.speaker: Rac.
sp.p: Spite your scoffing, sir, I am determined to do poor Stephen justice. I have written to him, and he'll be here to free himself before the week is out. I have had a letter from him, telling me that he is forced to seek work in another name.

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: Oh, by George! he changes his name, does he? That's rather unlucky, for such an immaculate chap. It's rather suspicious when an innocent man happens to have so many names!

sp.speaker: Rac.
sp.p: What!—what in the name of mercy was the poor lad to do? The masters against him on the one side, and the men against him on the other. He only wants to work for his bit of bread in peace. Can a man have no soul of his own—no mind of his own? Is he to be hunted down like a hare?

sp.speaker: Lou.
sp.p: Indeed, I pity him, and sincerely hope he will clear himself.

sp.speaker: Rac.
sp.p: He is sure to do so, young lady.

div.stage: (Louisa goes up stage. Tom joins her.)

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: All the surer for your refusing to say where he is, woman; eh?

sp.speaker: Rac.
sp.p: He shall not, through any act of mine, come back with the reproach of being brought. He shall come back of his own accord to clear himself, and put all those who have injured him and his good character to shame.

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: Nothwithstanding which, if he can be got hold of any sooner, he shall have an earlier chance of clearing himself.

div.stage: (Bound. and Grad. go up stage. Tom and Louisa come forward.)

sp.speaker: Tom.
sp.p: Don't forget to give me that money, Loo.

sp.speaker: Lou.
sp.p: What can you want so large a sum for?

sp.speaker: Tom.
sp.p: It's a desperate case, and the money I must have.

sp.speaker: Lou.
sp.p: Well, follow me.
You must be fatigued, my poor girl. In my father's house, I am free to exercise what hospitality I please. You shall have some refreshment. Now, Tom, you come along with me.

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: Come forward. I don't wish to pick a quarrel with you, Tom Gradgrind, about your daughter, whom I made Mrs. Bounderby, and might have done better if I had not; but, if she don't come home to-morrow by twelve at noon, I shall understand that she prefers to stay away, and shall send her boxes and furbelows over here; and you may take charge of her for the future.

sp.speaker: Mr. G.
sp.p: My dear Mr. Bounderby—

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: Don't dear me, sir. You will excuse me, sir, but I'd rather not be too dear. When I begin to be dear to a man, I generally find that his intention is to humbug me. Now, I don't mean to be humbugged.

sp.speaker: Mr. G.
sp.p: Mr. Bounderby, I will not submit to this language.

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: Lump it or leave it. It's what you and your beautiful daughter best understand.

sp.speaker: Mr. G.
sp.p: Say what you like to me, and of me, Mr. Bounderby, but be careful what you say of my child; she's an angel.

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: Is she? Of the black sort, I should say.

sp.speaker: Mr. G.
sp.p: This is atrocious. Bounderby, you are an old scoundrel!

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: Eh! I never allowed the boys in the street to call me that; and, to be called so to my face by a yellow, addle-pated, skulking rascal—

sp.speaker: Mr. G.
sp.p: I'll teach you to call me, your father-in-law, a rascal!

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: And I'll teach you, you old, scheming knave, to call Josiah Bounderby a scoundrel! Take that—and that!

div.stage: [Exeunt both in a violent rage, and cuffing each other.

div.head: SCENE IV.
div.stage: —A Landscape. A quantity of brushwood supposed to hide the chasm of an old pit.

sp.speaker: Bit.
sp.p: I cannot make it out. The appointed days have expired, and the individual does not come back. If the individual is not the thief, why does the individual keep away? In the name of a royal individual, I call upon the suspected party to come back! Come forth! come forth! The individual is silent. Silence gives consent. The suspected individual is the guilty man. Ha! here comes the individual's young woman! I won't be too hard upon her, for her individual's sake.
Cheer up, young woman; all may yet be well.

sp.speaker: Rac.
sp.p: I cannot help being mistrustful. I mistrust that some one, for bad purposes, has put Stephen out of the way. I mistrust that by his coming back of his own accord some one would be confounded, who, to prevent that has cruelly stopped him and put him out of the way.

sp.speaker: Bit.
sp.p: What, murder the individual? Do you think the individual has been foully dealt by?

sp.speaker: Rac.
sp.p: It is a thought; but—

sp.speaker: Bit.
sp.p: After all, the individual may have fallen ill upon the road, and in such there are many places on his journey, where sick individuals are taken in and done for.

sp.speaker: Rac.
sp.p: But he is in none of them. He has been sought for in all, but he is in none. He could walk the journey back with ease in two days.

sp.speaker: Bit.
sp.p: Yes, if the individual is a good pedestrian. It would take me a week; besides, I should stop to look at everything curious and singular in my individual way. Talking of curious things, see here's a fence, and broken—the wood is still green where it gave way. A footmark, too—the footmark of an individual; and, if my eyes don't deceive me, there's some individual's hat lying on the grass.

sp.speaker: Rac.
sp.p: A hat! For mercy's sake, 'pick it up. Is there a name in any part of it?

sp.speaker: Bit.
sp.p: The individual's name plain as a blackberry. S. B.—that's Stephen Blackpool, ain't it?

sp.speaker: Rac.
sp.p: Merciful heaven! he has been waylaid and killed. They have murdered him! They have murdered him!

sp.speaker: Bit.
sp.p: No, the individual's hat has no blood upon it.

sp.speaker: Rac.
sp.p: Search a little further. If you are frightened, I'll search myself. I will not leave a blade of grass unturned.

sp.speaker: Bit.
sp.p: Hold, rash individual, hold! In half a second more, you would have been down that horrible chasm.

sp.speaker: Rac.
sp.p: Oh, father of mercy, he is down there! Oh
, he is down there!

sp.speaker: Bit.
sp.p: Weak individual, stop these dreadful cries. Be patient.

sp.speaker: Rac.
sp.p: Patient, and the poor lad there! I almost fancy I hear him moaning at the bottom. If he has fallen in, we must not, will not, leave him in such a dreadful place for a moment.
sp.stage: (Runs agitatedly to the mouth of the pit.)
sp.p: Stephen, dear Stephen, poor Stephen!

He does not answer me. It has not reached the bottom. I cannot hear it fall. Oh, they have murdered, they have killed him—they have thrown him down this dreadful pit! Run for aid, run for assistance; do, good Bitzer, do.
Help! help!

sp.speaker: Bit.
sp.p: Here are several individuals coming. We will see what can be done.

sp.speaker: First Hand.
sp.p: What be the matter, neighbour? What's amiss?

sp.speaker: Bit.
sp.p: A certain individual's missing, and this individual
thinks that that individual has fallen in, or been thrown into, that pit by some wicked individuals.

sp.speaker: Rac.
sp.p: Oh, I know he's there; and if you'll only see, all that I have in the world, and all that I may ever earn, shall be yours if you will but try to save him.

sp.speaker: Second Hand.
sp.p: What is it you want us to do, lass?

sp.speaker: Rac.
sp.p: Descend to the bottom of the shaft. While there's life, there's hope. If you are men, if you are Christians, do this. Oh, my poor Stephen! my poor Stephen!

sp.speaker: First Hand.
sp.p: Descend to bottom o' the shaft. 'Tis impossible. The foul air would kill a hundred of us.

sp.speaker: Rac.
sp.p: Oh, don't say so—don't talk so! Here, take this necklace—take this ring.
Save him, save him!

sp.speaker: Second Hand.
sp.p: It's impossible, lass; there be no chance.

sp.speaker: Omnes.
sp.p: None—none in the least.

sp.speaker: Rac.
sp.p: Hard-hearted men! your fellow-workman is lying maimed and disabled there. In heaven's name, I call upon you to assist him!

sp.speaker: Third Hand.
sp.p: It be impossible. There does not exist a living soul foolhardy enough to venture down.

sp.speaker: Rac.
sp.p: There does. False hearts! coward hearts! there is one who will search the lowless depths of that abyss, and on the instant, too.

sp.speaker: First Hand.
sp.p: 'Twere sure destruction. Who be the fool?

sp.speaker: Rac.
sp.p: I—Rachel.

sp.speaker: Omnes.
sp.p: Rachel!

sp.speaker: Rac.
sp.p: Yes, fool though you call me. I'll descend wi' no other help than my firm belief in heaven to befriend and arm me.

div.stage: (Rushes to the mouth of pit, as scene closes.)

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
Mrs. S.
sp.p: The very woman, as I'm a bred and born lady.
Stop, you hag! I command you to stop!

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Bless me, what is the matter? Is the factory on fire?

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: I demand your name.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: I can't stop to tell you now. I shall be too late for the parliamentary.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: I insist upon knowing your name, and what you have got in that bundle.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Nothing.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: Nothing? No equivocation, woman. I must and will know.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Well, then, since you must, you shall. I promised Mrs. Jenkins that I would buy her good man a pair of corduroys, and I have done so. I must make haste, too, for he has to wear them at his club to-night. I can't stop a moment.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: You must stop—you shall stop. I have seen you hanging about the Bank, and I will know what you want there.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: That's a secret.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: Which I must and will extort from you.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: But you won't, though. I shall not talk to inquisitive strangers whom I do not care to know.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: What can such as you want at the Bank? I am sure you don't want to pay money in, and I know you have got none to draw out.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Well, well, that's of no consequence.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: Yes; but it is of consequence—of serious consequence.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: You'll excuse me. I shall be too late.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: No, you don't stir. You are an artful, designing, good-for-nothing old woman.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Good gracious! have I lived to be called good for nothing!

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: You are a very bad woman indeed. A disgrace to your sex—the companion of thieves, if not a thief yourself.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: A what?

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: I'll bandy no words with you. There, it's of no use you struggling.
Where's your companion—your base, wicked companion? Where's Stephen Blackpool?

sp.speaker: Mrs P.
sp.p: How should I know where he is.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: Oh, you base old woman! You know well enough you have had the impudence to wait outside while he robbed the Bank.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: I see the Bank robbed? I wait outside while any one did it? Not for worlds—no— no.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: I say yes, yes. I saw you waiting to give the alarm if anybody came. I've a great mind to shake your wicked old heart out, I have.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Don't ill-use—pray, don't ill-use me.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: Come peaceably along then. Come along.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Pray—pray, don't ill-use. me See, I have dropped the corduroys.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: Never mind the corduroys. Come along.

div.head: SCENE VI.
div.stage: —The Bottom of the Shaft. Stephen Blackpool discovered lying bruised and maimed on the earth. Large branches of wild brushwood spring out of the sides; and the light faintly descends from what appears to be a small opening at top, but which, in reality, is the top of the shaft.

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.p: Rachel, dear Rachel! Another day has passed, and still no hope of deliverance of any kind. Oh, 'tis hard to perish thus, and yet to see the refulgent sun shining o'er my head by day, and the light of moon by night! In vain I cry for help. I hear the noise o' the waggoners, and the merriment of the hands, as they pass by me in the high road to factory; but no one heeds me, and I must die, I 'spose, unheeded. The very birds that light on the trees and brushwood that broke my fall, seem to mock my agony! For days and nights my stiffened limbs have refused their office
; and yet I feel no pain now! Merciful God! the pain has left me, and—and—
—Father of heaven, I do stand upright again)

Were it but possible to reach yon opening—the height do make me giddy only looking at it! And, when I shout, what do I hear but the echo of my voice? What do I see but great big stones come toppling down, caused by the vibration—oh, Rachel, Rachel! shall I never see thy angel face again—hear thy consoling accents—or be I doomed to die a death which chills my stout heart to think upon? I'll make one desperate effort more to climb the top; and, if I fall, and be dashed to pieces, 'twill be a merciful death for Stephen, whose last prayer shall be for blessings on the head of Rachel!
sp.stage: (Stephen partly ascends the shaft by means of projecting stones. He seizes a branch, which seems to offer him a safe hold; it breaks, and he falls from a great height on to one of the projecting stones.)
sp.p: Heaven help me! now I can neither reach the top, nor safely fling myself to the bottom; and yet I have no good hold here. The stone already trembles! My weight be too great; and, if it fall, I shall be dashed to pieces!
No— no footing be firm enough; but the fall has broken my leg; I cannot put the one before the other.
Eh! what do I see? They be closing the top of shaft; and, merciful heavens, I shall be entombed alive!
Help, help! Rachel! Heaven look down, and pity me!

div.stage: (Rachel is making her way down from the top of the shaft.

sp.speaker: Rac.
sp.p: Stephen! dear Stephen!

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.p: That voice! Be this a dream? Do I hear right? Merciful Providence!

sp.speaker: Rac.
sp.p: Stephen, dear lad, hold on where thou art! I come to save thee!

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.p: Blessings be on thy head! I fear it be impossible.

div.stage: (Rachel descends, and, in descending, holds out her hands, and seems groping to catch at something. At last she clutches Stephen's extended hand.)

sp.speaker: Rac.
sp.p: Merciful Father! Stephen!

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.p: Rachel! be it thyself or spirit, lass? Oh, joy unutterable if be Rachel! Care, lass—care, lass; the slightest movement, and you will be dashed monny fathoms deep! Oh, for one ray of light to point out your danger!

sp.speaker: Rac.
sp.p: 'Tis here.
sp.stage: (Rachel strikes a light from a phosphorous-box she has brought with her, when their joint danger becomes apparent. A dreadful gulf seems between them. The rays of light fall and illumine the shaft.)
sp.p: Stephen! Stephen! I am here to save you!

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.p: Rachel, tak' my hand. When I got thy letter, I determined to clear myself at onny risk. I crossed to get back soon for thy sake; but, I mistook the way, lass, and fell into this pit, where I have been lying, wi' sore wounds and broken limbs, ever so monny days, insensible, Rachel—insensible; but heaven's good—heaven's will be done!

sp.speaker: Rac.
sp.p: There, there; lay your head upon my shoulder, and think only of home—your Rachel, and of happiness!

div.head: SCENE I.
div.stage: Enter MRS. SPARSIT, dragging on MRS. PEGLER, a crowd of hands and country people following.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: Come along, madam; come along quietly, or I'll have you handcuffed by the police. Leave her alone, everybody; let nobody touch her. She's my lawful prixe, and belongs to me. Come along, or I'll have you locked up in the cage.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Oh, rescue me, good people, rescue me! I have lost my leather purse; I have lost my corduroys; and, if you don't save me, I shall lose my reason.

sp.speaker: Second Hand.
sp.p: Shame, shame! Let the old lady go!

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: Not I, indeed. If any of you had had half the trouble to catch her that I've had, none of you would be for letting her go in a hurry.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Oh, Josiah! Save me, Josiah!

sp.speaker: Omnes.
sp.p: Shame! Shame!

div.stage: (Mrs. Sparsit drags Mrs. Pegler off, as the mob follow, and shout after her.)

sp.speaker: Bit.
Gra.
sp.p: My good man, it is not in my power. I have an objection, on principle, to employ persons who, heedlessly or thoughtlessly, throw themselves out of employment.

sp.speaker: Bit.
sp.p: I did not discharge myself. Mrs. Sparsit, sir—Mrs. Sparsit discharged me.

sp.speaker: Gra.
sp.p: There—there. I dare say Mrs. Sparsit had serious and sufficient reasons. But what on earth could possibly induce you to apply to me, above all men?

sp.speaker: Bit.
sp.p: Your interest and influence I know to be great, sir. There is Mr. Harthouse. If you would kindly say a word in my favour—

sp.speaker: Gra.
sp.p: I speak to Mr. Harthouse—I ask a favour from such a person! You little know the characteristics of the gentleman you are insulting by such a request. Once for all, I shall not.

sp.speaker: Bit.
sp.p: The bear!

sp.speaker: Gra.
sp.p: If you had solicited me to solve a problem rather above your comprehension, or to have translated a very difficult passage in Virgil, I might have done it, rather than you should have remained in total ignorance; but to have words with James Harthouse, is impossible— quite impossible.

sp.speaker: Bit.
sp.p: Lord bless you, sir! I don't want you to have any words with that individual, on my account. A letter of recommendation will answer the same purpose.

sp.speaker: Gra.
sp.p: Do you see that stone?

sp.speaker: Bit.
sp.p: Quite plain, sir.

sp.speaker: Gra.
sp.p: As well might you ask that immovable block of granite to descend at your bidding, take you on its surface, and carry you into the presence of the person you speak of, as myself to be the means of introducing you to each other. Go your way—

sp.speaker: Bit.
sp.p: Certainly; to be sure, sir; I'll go.
But, before I do go, by jingo, I'll make another attempt. I'll have another shy. Here goes!
I have been told sir, that you have occasionally helped a fellow-creature to get into a little way of business.

sp.speaker: Gra.
sp.p: Perhaps I have. I am ever ready to lend a helping hand to those who help themselves.

sp.speaker: Bit.
sp.p: I am that individual—that's precisely it, sir. Only give me the opportunity, and I'll help myself.

sp.speaker: Gra.
sp.p: Doubtless; but not at the expense of my pocket. You ought to be ashamed of yourself —a hale, and hearty young man like you— trying to live upon the industry of others. I do not see any bodily infirmity or disfigurement which incapacitates you from seeking employment. All I feel inclined to give you is advice— and I do that freely—seek honest employment.

sp.speaker: Bit.
sp.p: I have been seeking it, I am seeking it, and I will seek it—but I seek it under difficulties. Formerly, when I had a few perquisites, and the wherewith to treat a friend, nobody but had a smile for this individual; but now that I am likely to want a warm dinner, everybody looks cold upon me. The very day I received notice from Mrs. Sparsit, I heard that the station-master at the railway was ill, and I applied to get the appointment; but I was truly unlucky, for the doctor cured him; he recovered his health, and I lost my chance.

sp.speaker: Gra.
sp.p: A very proper rebuke from the Giver of all good for your indelicate haste to obtain a sick person's bread and butter. I am glad to hear he recovered.

sp.speaker: Bit.
sp.p: Well, as far as that goes, I am not. “Every one for himself” is my motto. But, sir, I am doomed to be unfortunate. I offered to sell a few of my books at a stall in the market-place this morning; but, as light reading is prohibited by order of the magistrates, I am still in the dark, and don't know what to do for the best. I am half-inclined to take to my father's old trade of breeches-making. And I would, too; but I fear, the very moment I did so, that useful and ornamental article might be dispensed with altogether. Nothing is so uncertain as fashion; otherwise, I always had a hankering to become a tailor.

sp.speaker: Gra.
sp.p: And a remunerative trade, too. Become one, and I promise you my custom.

sp.speaker: Bit.
sp.p: If you will only keep your word, sir! I an rather clever at turning a coat, sir; but so many great men have the knack of turning their own coats, now-a-days, that I may be forestalled.

sp.speaker: Gra.
sp.p: Pshaw! you are the most miserable, ill-conditioned dog I ever saw! I'll have nothing to do with you! Good day—good day!

sp.speaker: Bit.
sp.p: Thank you for nothing. Good day, indeed! It is a bad day, you mean; for that seems more in your way, the old curmudgeon! Faint heart never won fair lady. I'll summons up courage, and go back and ask Mrs. Sparsit to receive me into her service again. If she's the bred and born lady she pretends to be, she'll do, it of course. If not, I'll be off to London; but things are altered even there since I was a boy.

div.head: SCENE V.
div.stage: A crowd of persons discovered, anxiously surrounding the mouth of the pit, from which Stephen Blackpool and Rachel is drawn out. Rachel is still supporting Stephen. A great shout of exultation is heard as scene is discovered. In the midst BOUNDERBY rushes on.

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: Is Stephen Blackpool dead or alive?

sp.speaker: First Hand.
sp.p: Alive. Thanks to this heroic girl.

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: Then I arrest him for the robbery at the Bank. Officers, see that he does not escape.

sp.speaker: Omnes.
sp.p: Shame! Shame!

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: Ay; it's all very well of you to cry shame; but, bide a bit, and you'll see. Now, Mr. Blackpool, what have you to say?

sp.speaker: Rac.
sp.p: Speak, lad, speak, and shame him to his face.

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.p: If it were the last words I be permitted on earth to utter, I am innocent.

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: Make way there. There's another suspected person coming.

div.stage: Loud outcry. Enter MRS. SPARSIT, dragging on MRS. PEGLER, followed by MR. GRADGRIND, LOUISA, and TOM GRADGRIND.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: Now, Mr. Bounderby, sir—now you will be pleased to confess and admit the value of my services. I've got her at last. Rachel, you know this woman's name?

sp.speaker: Rac.
sp.p: Poor Mrs. Pegler!

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: I should say it is. Stand away, everbody.
It's of no use whispering to me. The law must take it's course. Mr. Bounderby, sir, this is the creature who was continually peeping in at the Bank windows.

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: What the devil do you mean by this, Mrs. Sparsit? I ask you, madam, if it is the conduct of a bred and born lady to be continually poking her nose into other people's affairs?

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: Oh, but I have obtained a clue to the robbery! This old artful creature is—

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: Mind your own business, madam. How dare you trouble yourself with my family matters?

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: My dear Josiah, my darling boy, I am not to blame; it's none of my fault. I told this cross old lady over and over again that I knew what she was doing would not be agreeable to you, but she would make me come.

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: What the devil did you let her bring you for? Couldn't you have knocked her teeth out, or have killed her, or something?

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Indeed and indeed, it is not my fault. I have always lived quiet and in secret, and never in my life have broken the condition on which you allowed me thirty pounds a-year. I have never said I was your mother. Oh, no; I have always kept at a respectful distance.

sp.speaker: Mr. G.
sp.p: I am surprised that you have the face to claim Mr. Bounderby after your unnatural— not to say inhuman—treatment of him!

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Me inhuman!—me unnatural to my own dear boy?

sp.speaker: Mr. G.
sp.p: Yes. Did you not desert him, and leave him to the care of his drunken grandmother?

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: I desert Josiah!

sp.speaker: Mr. G.
sp.p: Do you deny that he was born in a ditch?

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Born in a ditch! For shame, sir! He was born on two good flocks and a mattress—the best we could afford.

sp.speaker: Mr. G.
sp.p: Was he not left to play all day long in the gutter? And didn't he eat, I don't know how many horses in the disguise of polonies and saveloys.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Good gracious! How odd you talk! My dear boy knows, and will give you all to know, that I am his mother!

sp.speaker: Omnes.
sp.p: His mother!

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Yes; and a good mother to him. When his father died, and he was only eight years of age, I pinched myself for years to set him up in the world; and I recollect, on the day my Josiah was breeched—

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: Hold your tongue, will you? I say, you people, I am not bound to deliver you a lecture upon my family affairs before a mob of strangers, and in the presence of a suspected felon. I am not going to do it. In reference to the robbery at the Bank—my Bank, recollect, you people, my Bank, there has been a slight mistake made concerning my mother. If there had not been over-officiousnes, the old lady had been unmolested. I hate over-officiousness. Seize that over-officious old woman.

div.stage: (Points to Mrs. Sparsit, who is seized by Bitzer.)

sp.speaker: Mr. G.
sp.p: I, too, have officiousness. If there had not been a great deal too much of over-officiousness, this poor man would never have been charged with a crime of which he is totally innocent.

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: Innocent! What do you mean by that?

sp.speaker: Mr. G.
sp.p: What I say. There stands the culprit!

sp.speaker: Omnes.
sp.p: Tom Gradgrind!

sp.speaker: Mr. G.
sp.p: The same; but there was no robbery, after all. The money was removed by Tom for safety from one place to another, and is on the premises at this very time.

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: Where—where?

sp.speaker: Tom.
sp.p: In the third drawer of the iron safe with the brass padlock.
I put it there myself this morning with Loo's money.

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: I never thought to look there. Blackpool, I don't exactly know how to look you in the face; you have suffered a martyrdom through error and misconception. If you recover of your wounds, I am bound to make you amends, and I will—by Jove, I will! First, I'll give you Rachel for a wife. Secondly, I'll give her the whole of the £150 as a marriage portion, and that's not all I will do for the pair of you.

sp.speaker: Omnes.
sp.p: Huzza! huzza!

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.p: I am overjoyed, sir; but it's not your money which makes me gladsome—it is that restoration to character, which is far more valuable to me than shining gold, and without which all is a muddle.

sp.speaker: Bit.
sp.p: Mr. Bounderby, please sir, what am I to do with this individual? She's so precious strong, there's no holding her.

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: Let her go. Our society is not good enough for such a bred and born lady.

sp.speaker: Bit.
sp.p: Misguided individual, you may depart; but recollect the old school-copy, “Mind your own business,” small text, round-hand.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: The maledictions of the Powlers light upon the Bounderbys; and should they have any children
—which is not very likely— upon them also.

sp.speaker: Lou.
sp.p: Mr. Bounderby, I will now cheerfully accompany you back to the home you have provided for me, and I insist upon it that you allow your good mother to supply the place of Mrs. Sparsit.

sp.speaker: Bou.
sp.p: Agreed, Louisa; and that this may prove a week of happiness and rejoicing, I suspend work at the factory for seven days.
But I will pay full wages during all the time to every man, woman, and child; and my wife shall distribute £200 amongst you, to be spent in rejoicings at the safe return of the “Missing Hand.
